﻿ RC5 Algorithm Designed by Ronald Rivest in 1994.

Symmetric Key Block Cipher: The same key is used for both encryption and decryption.

Known for its simplicity, efficiency, and flexibility.

Used in software and hardware implementations.

﻿ Key Features Simplicity: 
Uses basic operations like XOR, modular addition, and data-dependent rotations.
Flexibility: 
Adjustable parameters for block size, key size, and number of rounds.
Security: 
Data-dependent rotations provide nonlinearity and resistance to cryptanalysis.
Efficiency: 
Designed to work efficiently on both software and hardware platforms.

﻿ Parameters of RC5 RC5 is basically denoted as RC5-w/r/b
Adjustable Parameters:
Block Size (w): Can be 32, 64, or 128 bits.
Number of Rounds (r): Can vary from 0 to 255 rounds (typically 12 or 16).
Key Size (b): Can range from 0 to 2040 bits (commonly 128-bit keys).

﻿ Structure of RC5 Feistel-Like Structure:
Block: The input block is divided into two halves A and B.
Operations per Round: Modular addition with subkeys.
Data-dependent rotations: XOR operations between the two halves.
Repeat for r rounds to generate ciphertext.

﻿ Algorithm The are three components of RC5
Key expansion algorithm
Encryption algorithm
Decryption algorithm

﻿ Encryption Process Initial Key Addition: Add subkeys S[0]] and S[1] to A and B respectively.
Rounds (for each of the r rounds):
Rotate A by an amount determined by B’s LSBs, then XOR with B.
Rotate B by an amount determined by modified A’s LSBs, then XOR with modified A.
Final Output: After r rounds, combine A and B to form ciphertext.
﻿ Encryption Process
﻿ Decryption

﻿ Decryption A >>> B
Bits in A are rotated to right by the amount  specified by lower log2(w) bits in B
﻿ Encryption and Decryption

﻿ RC5 Key Schedule Key Expansion:
Converts the original key into an array of 2(r+1) sub-keys.
Sub-key Generation:
Uses modular arithmetic to generate multiple sub-keys.
Sub-keys will be used sequentially (and only once each) during the encryption and decryption processes.
﻿ Key Expansion Algorithm

﻿ Security of RC5 Data-Dependent Rotations: 
Introduce nonlinearity, making the algorithm harder to break.
Adjustable Rounds: 
More rounds provide higher security.
Block and Key Sizes: 
Larger block and key sizes increase resistance to brute-force and cryptanalytic attacks.

﻿ Strengths of RC5 Highly Flexible: 
Adjustable parameters suit different security and performance needs.
Efficient: 
Uses simple operations (XOR, addition, rotation) that are fast and easy to implement.
Minimal Memory Usage: 
Suitable for environments with limited resources, like embedded systems.

﻿ Weaknesses of RC5 Vulnerable to Timing Attacks: 
The data-dependent rotations can be exploited in specific implementations.
Not as widely adopted: 
Although flexible, RC5 is not as popular as modern algorithms like AES.

﻿ Applications of RC5 OpenSSL: 
A widely used cryptographic library that includes RC5 as one of its supported algorithms.
SSH (Secure Shell): 
Can use RC5 for encrypting data transmitted over a network.IPSec (Internet Protocol Security): Can employ RC5 for encrypting and authenticating IP packets.
Database Encryption: 
RC5 can be used to encrypt data within databases to protect against unauthorized access.
Digital SIgnatures: 
RC5 can be used in conjunction with RSA for digital signatures to ensure data integrity and authenticity.

﻿ Public-Key Infrastructures (PKI) A model for creating, distributing, and revoking certificates based on the X.509. 
The Internet Engineering Task Force has created the Public-Key Infrastructure X.509 known as  PKIX.  pg 484
﻿ Duties of a PKI

﻿ Some important duties of PKI Certificates’ issuing, renewal, and revocation
As PKIX is X.509 dependent, the standard defines all certificate related duties.
Keys’ storage and update
PKI should provide key storage to members
Key updating facility on member’s demand
Providing services to other protocols
Internet security protocols, such as IPSec and TLS rely on the services by a PKI.
Providing access control
provide different levels of access to the information stored in its database
Eg: an organization PKI may provide access to the whole database for the top management, but limited access for employees.

﻿ Trust Model of PKI It is not possible to have just one CA issuing all certificates for all users in the world.
There should be many CAs, each responsible for creating, storing, issuing, and revoking a limited number of certificates. 
PKI therefore establishes a framework called as Trust Model for building trust and security in digital communications.
The trust model defines rules that specify how a user can verify a certificate received from a CA.

﻿ PKI Hierarchical Model In this model, there is a tree-type structure with a root CA. 
The root CA has a self-signed, self-issued certificate; it needs to be trusted by other CAs and users for the system to work. 
The number of levels can be more than three in a real.
﻿ PKI Hierarchical Model

﻿ PKI Hierarchical Model The CA (the root) has signed certificates for CA1, CA2, and CA3.
CA1 has signed certificates for User1, User2, and User3; and so on. 
PKI uses the following notation to mean the certificate issued by authority X for entity Y. 𝑿≪𝒀≫
﻿ Chrome Browser Certificate List

﻿ Mesh Model The hierarchical model may work for an organization or a small community.
A larger community may need several hierarchical structures connected together. 
One method is to use a mesh model to connect the roots together. 
In this model, each root is connected to every other root.
﻿ Mesh Model

﻿ Mesh Model The mesh structure connects only roots together
Each root has its own hierarchical structure, shown by a triangle. 
The certifications between the roots are cross-certificates; 
Each root certifies all other roots, which means there are N (N − 1) certificates.

﻿ Web of Trust (WoT) Model WoT is a decentralized trust model used in Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) 
Individuals and organizations can issue certificates to each other, creating a network of trust relationships. 
This differs from the traditional hierarchical trust model where a single Certificate Authority (CA) is responsible for issuing and managing all certificates.

﻿ How the Web of Trust works Certificate Issuance: An individual or organization can issue a certificate to another entity, signing it with their private key.
Certificate Validation: When one entity wants to verify the authenticity of another entity's digital signature, they check the certificate associated with the signature. The certificate is validated by following the trust path through the web of trust.
Reputation Systems: Users can rate the trustworthiness of other users based on their interactions and experiences. This information can be used to assess the credibility of certificates issued by different entities.
Revocation: If a certificate is compromised or no longer valid, the issuing entity can publish revocation information. Other users can then update their trust databases accordingly.

﻿ Advantages of the Web of Trust model Resilience: The decentralized nature of the WoT makes it more resilient to attacks on a single CA.
Flexibility: It allows for more flexible trust relationships and can accommodate a wider range of use cases.
Privacy: The WoT can provide a higher level of privacy compared to the hierarchical trust model, as there is no central authority collecting and storing user data.
Community-Driven: The WoT is often driven by communities of users who collaborate to maintain and improve the system.

﻿ Disadvantages of the Web of Trust model Complexity: The WoT can be more complex to manage and understand compared to the hierarchical trust model.
Scalability: It may be more difficult to scale the WoT to handle large numbers of users and certificates.
Security: The security of the WoT depends on the trustworthiness of individual users and the effectiveness of reputation systems.

﻿ Applications Email encryption: The WoT can be used to encrypt and decrypt emails, ensuring privacy and confidentiality.
File sharing: It can be used to securely share files between individuals and organizations.
Digital signatures: The WoT can be used to verify the authenticity and integrity of digital documents.

  22nd Oct  2024 pg 441

﻿ Remote User Authentication Protocols User authentication also known as entity authentication is a technique designed to let one party prove the identity of another party. 
An entity can be a person, a process, a client, or a server.
The entity whose identity needs to be proved is called the claimant.
The party that tries to prove the identity of the claimant is called the verifier.
Commonly used techniques,
Something known
Something possessed
Something inherent

﻿ Remote User Authentication Protocols Something known
 This is a secret known only by the claimant that can be checked by the verifier. 
Examples are a password, a PIN, a secret key, and a private key.
Something possessed
 This is something that can prove the claimant’s identity.
Examples are a passport, a driver’s license, an identification card, a credit card, and a smart card.
Something inherent
This is an inherent characteristic of the claimant. 
Examples are conventional signatures, fingerprints, voice, facial characteristics, retinal pattern, and handwriting.

﻿ PASSWORDS The simplest and oldest method of entity authentication is the password-based authentication
the password is something that the claimant knows.
A password is used when a user needs to access a system to use the system’s resources (login). 
Each user has a user identification that is public, and a password that is private. 
We can divide these authentication schemes into two groups,
The fixed password 
The one-time password

﻿ The Fixed Password A password that is used over and over again for every access.
First Approach: User ID and password file
Second Approach: Hashing the password
Third Approach: Salting the password
Fourth Approach: Combination

﻿ First Approach: User ID and password file The system keeps a table (a file) that is sorted by user identification. 
To access the system resources, the user sends her user identification and password, in plaintext, to the system.
The system uses the identification to find the password in the table. If the password sent by the user matches the password in the table, access is granted; otherwise, it is denied.

﻿ Attacks on the First Approach Eavesdropping: Eve can watch Alice when she types her password. Most systems, as a security measure, do not show the characters a user types. Eavesdropping can take a more sophisticated form. Eve can use key loggers.
Stealing a password: Eve tries to physically steal Alice’s password. This can be prevented if Alice does not write down the password and instead she just commits it to memory. For this reason the password should be very simple or else related to something familiar to Alice. But this makes the password vulnerable to other types of attacks.

﻿ Attacks on the First Approach Accessing a password file: 
Eve can hack into the system and get access to the ID/ password file. Eve can read the file and find Alice’s password or even change it. To prevent this type of attack, the file can be read/write protected. However, most systems need this type of file to be readable by the public. The second approach can protect the file from this type of attack.

﻿ Attacks on the First Approach Guessing: 
Using a guessing attack, Eve can log into the system and try to guess Alice’s password by trying different combinations of characters. 
The password is particularly vulnerable if the user is allowed to choose a short password (a few characters). 
It is also vulnerable if Alice has chosen something trivial, such as her birthday, her child’s name, or the name of her favourite actor. 
To prevent guessing, a long random password is recommended, something that is not very obvious. 
However, the use of such a random password may also create a problem. 
Because she could easily forget such a password, Alice might store a copy of it somewhere, which makes the password subject to stealing.

﻿ Second Approach: Hashing the password A more secure approach is to store the hash of the password (instead of the plaintext password) in the password file. 
Any user can read the contents of the file, but, because the hash function is a one-way function, it is almost impossible to guess the value of the password.

﻿ Second Approach: Hashing the password When the user sends the ID and the password, the system creates a hash of the password and then compares the hash value with the one stored in the file. 
If there is a match, the user is granted access; otherwise, access is denied. 
In this case, the file does not need to be read protected.

﻿ Attack on the Second Approach Dictionary Attack 
In this attack, Eve is interested in finding one password, regardless of the user ID. 
For example, if the password is 6 digits, Eve can create a list of 6-digit numbers (000000 to 999999), and then apply the hash function to every number; the result is a list of one million hashes.
She can then get the password file and search the second-column entries to find a match. 
This could be programmed and run offline on Eve’s private computer.
After a match is found, Eve can go online and use the password to access the system. 
The third approach shows how to make this attack more difficult.

﻿ Third Approach: Salting the password When the password string is created, a random string, called the salt, is concatenated to the password. 
The salted password is then hashed. 
The ID, the salt, and the hash are then stored in the file. 
Now, when a user asks for access, the system extracts the salt, concatenates it with the received password, makes a hash out of the result, and compares it with the hash stored in the file. 
If there is a match, access is granted; otherwise, it is denied
﻿ Third Approach: Salting the password

﻿ Third Approach: Salting the password Salting makes the dictionary attack more difficult. 
If the original password is 6 digits and the salt is 4 digits, then hashing is done over a 10-digit value. 
This means that Eve now needs to make a list of 10 million items and create a hash for each of them.
The list of hashes has 10 million entries, and the comparison takes much longer. 
Salting is very effective if the salt is a very long random number. 
The UNIX operating system uses a variation of this method.

﻿ Fourth Approach: Combination Two identification techniques are combined. 
Example: use of an ATM card with a PIN (personal identification number)
The card belongs to the category “something possessed ” and the PIN belongs to the category “something known”. 
The PIN is a password that enhances the security of the card. 
If the card is stolen, it cannot be used unless the PIN is known. 
The PIN number, however, is traditionally very short so it is easily remembered by the owner.
This makes it vulnerable to the guessing type of attack.

﻿ The one-time password A password that is used only once. 
This kind of password makes eavesdropping and salting useless.
The user and the system agree upon a list of passwords. 
Each password on the list can be used only once. 
Drawbacks: 
The system and the user must keep a long list of passwords. 
If the user does not use the passwords in sequence, the system needs to perform a long search to find the match.

﻿ CHALLENGE-RESPONSE In password authentication, the claimant proves his/her identity by demonstrating that he/she knows a secret, the password.
In challenge-response authentication, the claimant proves that he/she knows a secret without sending it. 
In other words, the claimant does not send the secret to the verifier; the verifier either has it or finds it.
The technique needs Challenge and Response.

﻿ CHALLENGE-RESPONSE The challenge is a time-varying value such as a random number or a timestamp that is sent by the verifier.
The claimant applies a function to the challenge and sends the result, called a response, to the verifier. 
The response shows that the claimant knows the secret.

﻿ CHALLENGE-RESPONSE Rest part is left as Self study.

﻿ IP level Security Introduction to IPSec: 
IP Security (IPSec) is a collection of protocols designed by the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) to provide security for a packet at the network level.

﻿ Need of Security at IP Layer Security at the application & transport layers may not be enough in some cases. 
Not all client/server programs are protected at the application layer; for example, PGP and S/MIME protect only electronic mail. 
Not all client/server programs at the application layer use the service of TCP to be protected by SSL or TLS; some programs use the service of UDP. 
Many applications, such as routing protocols, directly use the service of IP; they need security services at the IP layer.

rects.text: Need of Security at IP Layer

slides.text:
﻿ Applications of IPSec To enhance the security of those client/server programs, such as electronic mail, that use their own security protocols. 
To enhance the security of those client/server programs, such as HTTP, that use the security services provided at the transport layer. 
It can provide security for those client/server programs that do not use the security services provided at the transport layer. 
It can provide security for node-to-node communication programs such as routing protocols.

﻿ Applications of IPSec IPsec provides the capability to secure communications across a LAN, across private and public WANs, and across the Internet. 

Practical Applications: 
Secure branch office connectivity over the Internet
Secure remote access over the Internet
Establishing extranet and intranet connectivity with partners
Enhancing electronic commerce security

﻿ Modes of IPSec IPSec operates in two different modes:
Transport mode 
Tunnel mode

﻿ IPSec in transport mode In transport mode, IPSec protects what is delivered from the transport layer to the network layer. 
IPSec in transport mode does not protect the IP header. It only protects the information coming from the transport layer.
﻿ IPSec Transport mode in action

﻿ IPSec in Tunnel Mode In tunnel mode, IPSec protects the entire IP packet. 
It takes an IP packet, including the header, applies IPSec security methods to the entire packet, and then adds a new IP header.
IPSec in tunnel mode protects the original IP header.
﻿ IPSec Tunnel mode in action
﻿ Transport mode versus Tunnel mode

﻿ Transport mode versus Tunnel mode Transport mode is used for end - to- end communication between two hosts .




Tunnel mode is used when one or both ends of a security association (SA) are a security gateway, such as a firewall or router that implements IPsec.

﻿ AH Protocol operation The Authentication Header (AH) Protocol is designed to authenticate the source host and to ensure the integrity of the payload carried in the IP packet. 
The protocol uses a hash function and a symmetric key to create a message digest; the digest is inserted in the authentication header. 
The AH is then placed in the appropriate location, based on the mode (transport or tunnel). 
When an IP datagram carries an authentication header, the original value in the protocol field of the IP header is replaced by the value 51.

﻿ AH Protocol operation The addition of an authentication header follows these steps:
An AH is added to the payload with authentication data field set to 0.
Padding may be added for a particular hashing algorithm
Hashing is based on the total packet. However only those fields of the IP header that do not change during transmission are included in the calculation of the message digest i.e. authentication data.
The authentication data is inserted in the authentication header.
The IP header is added after changing the value of the protocol filed to 51.

﻿ Description of every field of AH protocol Next header: The 8 bit header field defines the type of payload carried by the IP datagrams (such as TCP , UDP, ICMP ). The process copies the value of the protocol field in the IP datagram to this field. The value of the protocol field in the new IP datagram is now set to 51 to show that the packet carried an AH.
Payload length: It defines the length of the AH in 4 -byte multiples.

Security Parameter index: The 32 bit SPI field plays the role of a virtual circuit identifier & is the same for all packets sent during a connection called Security Association (SA).
Sequence Number: A 32 bit sequence number provides ordering information for a sequence of datagrams. It prevents a playback. Sequence number is not repeated even if a packet is retransmitted.
Authentication data: This field is the result of applying a hash function to the entire IP datagram except for the fields that are changed during transit.

﻿ Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) AH protocol do not provide privacy, only source authentication and data integrity.
IPSec later defined ESP protocol.
It provides source authentication , integrity & privacy.
It adds a header & trailer.
ESP's authentication data are added at the end of the packet which makes its calculation easier.
﻿ Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)

﻿ ESP operation When an IP datagram carries an ESP header & trailer, the value of the protocol field in the IP header is 50.
A field inside the ESP trailer (next header field) holds the original value of the protocol field (the type of payload being carried by the IP datagram such as TCP or UDP).
ESP procedure follows the following steps :
An ESP trailer is added to the payload.
The payload & the trailer are encrypted.
The ESP header is added.
The ESP header, payload & ESP trailer are used to create the authentication data.
The authentication data are added to the end of the ESP trailer.
The IP header is added after changing the protocol value of 50.
﻿ IPSec services

﻿ Comparison Transport mode provides protection primarily for upper-layer protocols. That is, transport mode protection extends to the payload of an IP packet.
Examples include a TCP or UDP segment or an ICMP packet, all of which operate directly above IP in a host protocol stack. 
Typically, ESP in transport mode encrypts and optionally authenticates the IP payload but not the IP header. AH in transport mode authenticates the IP payload and selected portions of the IP header. Tunnel mode provides protection to the entire IP packet. To achieve this, after the AH or ESP fields are added to the IP packet, the entire packet plus security fields is treated as the payload of new outer IP packet with a new outer IP header. 
The entire original, inner, packet travels through a tunnel from one point of an IP network to another; no routers along the way are able to examine the inner IP header.
The unprotected packets generated by such hosts are tunneled through external networks by tunnel mode SAs set up by the IPSec software in the firewall or secure router at the boundary of the local network. 
ESP in tunnel mode encrypts and optionally authenticates the entire inner IP packet, including the inner IP header. AH in tunnel mode authenticates the entire inner IP packet and selected portions of the outer IP header

﻿ Summary IPSec Security Architecture DOI (Domain of Interpretation): DOI is the identifier that supports both AH and ESP protocols. It contains values needed for documentation related to each other. 
Key Management: Key Management contains the document that describes how the keys are exchanged between sender and receiver.

﻿ IPSec Architecture Notes IPSec (Internet Protocol Security) is a suite of protocols designed to secure IP network communications. 
Its architecture is centered around two primary protocols: 
Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) and Authentication Header (AH).
Key Components
Security Association (SA): A logical connection between two endpoints that defines the security parameters for communication.
Internet Key Exchange (IKE): A protocol used to negotiate, establish, and manage SAs.
ESP: Provides confidentiality, integrity, and optional authentication for IP packets. It encapsulates the original IP packet within a new IP header, encrypts the payload, and optionally adds an integrity check.
AH: Provides data integrity and authentication. It adds an authentication header to the IP packet, ensuring that the packet hasn't been modified in transit and verifying the sender's identity.
Modes of Operation
IPSec supports two modes of operation:
Transport Mode: Only the IP payload is protected. This is suitable for applications that already encapsulate their data within IP packets.
Tunnel Mode: The entire IP packet (including the original IP header) is protected. This is useful for protecting traffic between network boundaries.

﻿ IPSec Architecture SA and IKE are two fundamental components of the Internet Protocol Security (IPSec) protocol suite, used to establish secure communication channels over IP networks.
Security Association (SA)
Definition: An SA is a logical connection between two endpoints that specifies the security parameters used for communication.
Key Elements:
Protocols: The protocols used for data encryption, integrity checking, and key management.
Algorithms: The specific cryptographic algorithms employed for these functions.
Keys: The secret keys used to encrypt and decrypt data.
Lifetime: The duration for which the SA remains active.
Purpose: Provides a framework for secure communication between two parties. Defines the security services to be applied to data packets.Ensures confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity of data.

﻿ IPSec Architecture Internet Key Exchange (IKE)
Definition: IKE is a protocol used to negotiate, establish, and manage SAs.
Key Functions:
Authentication: Verifies the identities of the communicating parties.
Key Generation: Creates cryptographic keys for use in the SA.
SA Establishment: Sets up the SA with the agreed-upon security parameters.
SA Management: Updates or terminates SAs as needed.
Phases:
Phase 1: Establishes a secure channel between the two parties, typically using public key cryptography for authentication and key exchange.
Phase 2: Negotiates the parameters for the SA, including encryption algorithms, authentication methods, and key lifetimes.
In summary, SA provides the framework for secure communication, while IKE is responsible for creating and managing these SAs. Together, they form the core of IPSec, ensuring the confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity of data transmitted over IP networks.

﻿ Need of Transport Level Security Transport layer security provides end-to-end security services for applications that use a reliable transport layer protocol such as TCP. 
The idea is to provide security services for transactions on the Internet. 
For example, when a customer shops online, following security services are desired:
The customer needs to be sure that the server belongs to the actual vendor, not an impostor. The customer does not want to give an impostor her credit card number (entity authentication).
The customer and the vendor need to be sure that the contents of the message are not modified during transmission (message integrity).
The customer and the vendor need to be sure that an impostor does not intercept sensitive information such as a credit card number (confidentiality).

﻿ Transport level security Two protocols are dominant today for providing security at the transport layer: 
Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) Protocol 
Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol
TLS is an IETF’s version of the SSL.  Security Layer Transport Layer Network Layer

﻿ Example of Transport level Security Transport level Security provide server and client authentication, data confidentiality, and data integrity. 
Application-layer client/server programs, such as Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), that use the services of TCP can encapsulate their data in SSL packets.
If the server and client are capable of running SSL (or TLS) programs then the client can use the URL https://… instead of http://… to allow HTTP messages to be encapsulated in SSL (or TLS) packets.

﻿ Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) Protocol SSL is designed to provide security & compression to data from the application layer. 
Typically, SSL can receive data from any application layer protocol, but usually the protocol is HTTP. 
The data received from the application is compressed (optional), signed, and encrypted. 
The data is then passed to a reliable transport layer protocol such as TCP. 
Netscape developed SSL in 1994. 
Versions 2 and 3 were released in 1995. 
we discuss the latest SSLv3.

﻿ SSL Protocol Architecture SSL connection and session

Connection: A connection is a network transport that provides a suitable type of service, such connections are transient, peer-to-peer relationships, associated with one session

Session: An SSL session is an association between a client and a server, created by the Handshake Protocol. 
Sessions define a set of cryptographic security parameters, which can be shared among multiple connections. 
Sessions are used to avoid the expensive negotiation of new security parameters for each connection.

﻿ SSL Record Protocol Services SSL Record Protocol defines two services for SSL connections:
Message Integrity: The Handshake Protocol defines a shared secret key that is used to form a message authentication code (MAC), similar to HMAC
Confidentiality: The Handshake Protocol defines a shared secret key that is used for conventional encryption of SSL payloads. The message is compressed before being concatenated with the MAC and encrypted, with a range of ciphers being supported
﻿ SSL Record Protocol Operation
﻿ Record Protocol Header

﻿ SSL Record Protocol Operation The first step is fragmentation. Each upper-layer message is fragmented into blocks of 2^14bytes (16384 bytes) or less. 
Next, compression is optionally applied. Compression must be lossless and may not increase the content length by more than 1024 bytes. 
The next step in processing is to compute a message authentication code over the compressed data.
Next, the compressed message plus the MAC are encrypted using symmetric encryption. 
The final step of SSL Record Protocol processing is to prepare a header consisting of the following fields:
Content Type (8 bits): The higher-layer protocol used to process the enclosed fragment.
Major Version (8 bits): Indicates major version of SSL in use. For SSLv3, the value is 3.
Minor Version (8 bits): Indicates minor version in use. For SSLv3, the value is 0.
Compressed Length (16 bits): The length in bytes of the plaintext fragment (or compressed fragment if compression is used).

﻿ SSL Handshake Protocol The Handshake Protocol uses messages to negotiate the cipher suite, to authenticate the server to the client and the client to the server if needed
To exchange information for building the cryptographic secrets. 
The handshaking is done in four phases,
﻿ SSL Handshake Protocol

﻿ SSL Change Cipher Spec Protocol The negotiation of the cipher suite and the generation of cryptographic secrets are formed gradually during the Handshake Protocol.
SSL mandates that the parties cannot use  these parameters or secrets until they have sent or received a special message, the ChangeCipherSpec message
The sender and the receiver need two states,
The pending state, keeps track of the parameters and secrets. 
The active state, holds parameters and secrets used by the Record Protocol to sign/verify or encrypt/decrypt messages.
The ChangeCipherSpec Protocol defines the process of moving values between the pending and active states.

﻿ SSL Alert Protocol SSL uses the Alert Protocol for reporting errors and abnormal conditions. 
It has only one message type, the Alert message, that describes the problem and its level (warning or fatal).

﻿ Generation of Cryptographic Secrets in TLS The generation of cryptographic secrets is more complex in TLS than in SSL. 
TLS first defines two functions: 
Data-expansion function
Pseudorandom function

﻿ Data-Expansion Function of TLS It uses a predefined HMAC (either MD5 or SHA-1) to expand a secret into a longer one. 
This function can be considered a multiple section function, where each section creates one hash value. 
The extended secret is the concatenation of the hash values. 
Each section uses two HMACs, a secret and a seed
The data-expansion function is the chaining of as many sections as required. 
However, to make the next section dependent on the previous, the second seed is actually the output of the first HMAC of the previous section
﻿ Data-Expansion Function of TLS

﻿ Pseudorandom Function (PRF) of TLS PRF is a combination of two data-expansion functions, one using MD5 and the other SHA-1. 
PRF takes three inputs, a secret, a label, and a seed. 
The label and seed are concatenated and serve as the seed for each data expansion function. 
The secret is divided into two halves; each half is used as the secret for each data-expansion function. 
The output of two data-expansion functions is exclusive ORed together to create the final expanded secret. 
Because the hashes created from MD5 and SHA-1 are of different sizes, extra sections of MD5-based functions must be created to make the two outputs the same size
﻿ Pseudorandom Function (PRF) of TLS

﻿ ‘Pre-master Secret’ Generation in SSL & TLS The generation of the pre-master secret in TLS is exactly the same as in SSL.
SSL defines six key-exchange methods to establish this premaster secret: NULL, RSA, anonymous Diffie-Hellman, ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, fixed Diffie-Hellman, and Fortezza
TLS supports five methods: NULL, RSA, anonymous Diffie-Hellman, ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, fixed Diffie-Hellman

﻿ ‘Master Secret’ Generation in TLS TLS uses the PRF function to create the ‘master secret’ from the ‘pre-master secret’
This is achieved by using,
‘‘pre-master secret’’ as the ‘secret’
“master secret” as the ‘label’
concatenation of the ‘client random number’ and ‘server random number’ as the ‘seed’. 
Note that the label is actually the ASCII code of the string “master secret”. 
In other words, the label defines the output we want to create, the master secret.
﻿ ‘Master Secret’ Generation in TLS

﻿ ‘Key Material’ generation in TLS TLS uses PRF function to create the key material from the master secret. 
This is achieved by using, 
the secret as the master secret
the label is the string “key expansion”
the seed is the concatenation of the server random number and the client random number

﻿ HTTPS HTTPS refers to the combination of HTTP and SSL/TLS to implement secure communication between a web browser and web server.
The principal difference seen by a user of a web browser is that URL addresses begin with https:// rather than http://.
A normal HTTP connection uses port 80. If HTTPS is specified, port 443 is used, which invokes SSL/TLS.
When HTTPS is used , the following elements of the communication are encrypted:
URL of the requested document
Contents of the document
Contents of browser forms
Cookies sent from browser to server and from server to browser.
Contents of HTTP header.

﻿ HTTPS Connection Initiation:
The client initiates a connection to the server on the appropriate port and then sends the TLS Client Hello to begin the TLS handshake.
When the TLS handshake is finished, the client may then initiate the first HTTP request.
All HTTP data is to be sent as TLS application data.
Connection Closure:
An HTTP client or server can indicate the closing of a connection by including the following line in an HTTP record: Connection: close.
The closure of an HTTPS connection requires that TLS close the connection with the peer TLS entity on the remote side, which will invoke closing the underlying TCP connection.
At the TLS level, the proper way to close a connection is for each side to use the TLS alert protocol to send a close_notify alert.
﻿ SECURE SHELL Secure Shell (SSH) is a protocol for secure network communications designed to be relatively simple and inexpensive to implement.

﻿ Email Security SECURE/MULTIPURPOSE INTERNET MAIL EXTENSION 
(S/MIME)

﻿ SECURE/MULTIPURPOSE INTERNET MAIL EXTENSION (S/MIME) It’s a security enhancement to the MIME Internet e-mail format standard based on technology from RSA Data Security. 
To understand S/MIME, we need first to have a general understanding of the underlying e-mail format that it uses, namely MIME. 
But to understand the significance of MIME, we need to go back to the traditional e-mail format standard, RFC 822(SMTP), which is still in common use. 
The most recent version of this format specification is RFC 5322 (Internet Message Format).

﻿ RFC 5322 RFC 5322 defines a format for text messages that are sent using electronic mail
In the RFC 5322 context, messages are viewed as having an envelope and contents. 
The RFC 5322 standard applies only to the contents. 
A message consists of some number of header lines (the header) followed by unrestricted text (the body). 
The header is separated from the body by a blank line.
A header line usually consists of a keyword, followed by a colon, followed by the keyword’s arguments; the format allows a long line to be broken up into several lines.
The most frequently used keywords are From, To, Subject, and Date etc
﻿ RFC 5322 Email format

﻿ MIME Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions
MIME is an extension to the RFC 5322 framework that is intended to address some of the problems and limitations of the use of Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP), defined in RFC 821, and RFC 5322 for electronic mail
Following are limitations of the SMTP/5322 scheme. 
SMTP cannot transmit executable files & binary objects. 
SMTP do not support national language characters.
SMTP servers has size restriction for email messages.
SMTP gateways that translate between ASCII and the character code EBCDIC do not use a consistent set of mappings, resulting in translation problems.
SMTP gateways to X.400 electronic mail networks cannot handle non textual data included in X.400 messages.

﻿ MIME Overview  The MIME specification includes the following elements.
Five new message header fields are defined, which can be included in an RFC 5322 header. These fields provide information about the body of the message.
Several content formats are defined, thus standardizing representations that support multimedia electronic mail.
Transfer encodings are defined that enable the conversion of any content format into a form that is protected from alteration by the mail system.

﻿ MIME The five header fields defined in MIME are
MIME-Version: Must have the parameter value 1.0. This field indicates that the message conforms to RFCs 2045 and 2046.
Content-Type: Describes the data contained in the body with sufficient detail that the receiving user agent can pick an appropriate agent or mechanism to represent the data to the user or otherwise deal with the data in an appropriate manner.
Content-Transfer-Encoding: Indicates the type of transformation that has been used to represent the body of the message in a way that is acceptable for mail transport.
Content-ID: Used to identify MIME entities uniquely in multiple contexts.
Content-Description: A text description of the object with the body; this is useful when the object is not readable (e.g., audio data).

﻿ MIME The material in this presentation belongs to St. Francis Institute of Technology and is solely for educational purposes. Distribution and modifications of the content is prohibited. MIME Content Types
The bulk of the MIME specification is concerned with the definition of a variety of content types. 
This reflects the need to provide standardized ways of dealing with a wide variety of information representations in a multimedia environment.
There are seven different major types of content and a total of 15 subtypes. 
In general, a content type declares the general type of data, and the subtype specifies a particular format for that type of data
﻿ MIME Content Types
﻿ MIME Content Types continued..

﻿ MIME Email Format For the multipart/alternative subtype, the various parts are different representations of the same information. The following is an example:

From: Nathaniel Borenstein <nsb@bellcore.com>
To: Ned Freed <ned@innosoft.com>
Subject: Formatted text mail
MIME-Version: 1.0
Content-Type: multipart/alternative;
boundary = boundary42
—boundary42
Content-Type: text/plain; charset = us-ascii
. . . plain text version of message goes here . . ..
—boundary42
Content-Type: text/enriched
. . . RFC 1896 text/enriched version of same message
goes here . . .
—boundary42—

﻿ MIME MIME Transfer Encodings 
provide reliable delivery across the largest range of environments.
This field can take on six values. However, three of these values (7bit, 8bit, and binary) indicate that no encoding has been done but provide some information about the nature of the data. 
For SMTP transfer, it is safe to use the 7bit form. The 8bit and binary forms may be usable in other mail transport contexts. 
The x-token, indicates that some other encoding scheme is used for which a name is to be supplied. This could be a vendor-specific or application-specific scheme. 
The quoted-printable transfer encoding is useful when the data consists largely of octets that correspond to printable ASCII characters. 
The base64 transfer encoding (known as radix-64 encoding) is a common one for encoding arbitrary binary data in such a way as to be invulnerable to the processing by mail-transport programs.
﻿ MIME Transfer Encodings

﻿ MIME Native & Canonical Form Canonical Form 
An important concept in MIME and S/MIME is that of canonical form.  
Canonical form is a format, appropriate to the content type, that is standardized for use between systems. 
This is in contrast to native form, which is a format that may be peculiar to a particular system.
﻿ MIME Native & Canonical Form

﻿ Secure/MIME or S/MIME S/MIME adds some new content types to include security services to the MIME. 
All of these new types include the parameter “application/pkcs7-mime” in which “pkcs” defines “Public Key Cryptography Specification.”
Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
To define how security services, such as confidentiality or integrity, can be added to MIME content types, S/MIME has defined Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS). 
The syntax defines the exact encoding scheme for each content type.

﻿ S/MIME data content Types Encrypted-Data Content Type

This type is used to create an encrypted version of any content type. 
Although this looks like the enveloped-data content type, the encrypted-data content type has no recipient. 
It can be used to store the encrypted data instead of transmitting it. 
The process is very simple, the user employs any key (normally driven from the password) and any algorithm to encrypt the content. 
The encrypted content is stored without including the key or the algorithm. 
The object created is called encryptedData.

﻿ Secure/MIME Functionality S/MIME provides the following functions:
Enveloped data: This consists of encrypted content of any type and encrypted content encryption keys for one or more recipients.
Signed data: A digital signature is formed by taking the message digest of the content to be signed and then encrypting that with the private key of the signer. The content plus signature are then encoded using base64 encoding. A signed data message can only be viewed by a recipient with S/MIME capability.
Clear-signed data: As with signed data, a digital signature of the content is formed. However, in this case, only the digital signature is encoded using base64. As a result, recipients without S/MIME capability can view the message content, although they cannot verify the signature.
Signed and enveloped data: Signed-only and encrypted-only entities may be nested, so that encrypted data may be signed and signed data or clear-signed data may be encrypted.

﻿ S/MIME Cryptographic Algorithms  S/MIME defines several cryptographic algorithms.
The term “must” means an absolute requirement.
The term “should” means recommendation.

﻿ S/MIME Cryptographic Algorithms  S/MIME uses the following terminology taken from RFC 2119 to specify the requirement level:
MUST: The definition is an absolute requirement of the specification. An implementation must include this feature or function to be in conformance with the specification.
SHOULD: There may exist valid reasons in particular circumstances to ignore this feature or function, but it is recommended that an implementation include the feature or function.
S/MIME incorporates three public-key algorithms. The Digital Signature Standard 
S/MIME lists Diffie-Hellman as the preferred algorithm for encrypting session keys; in fact, S/MIME uses a variant of Diffie-Hellman that does provide encryption/decryption, known as ElGamal.
For message encryption, three-key triple DES (tripleDES) is recommended.
﻿ S/MIME Cryptographic Algorithms

﻿ Summary S/MIME protocol is an enhancement of the Multipurpose Internet Mail Extension (MIME) protocol
S/MIME allows non-ASCII data to be sent through e-mail. 
S/MIME adds some new content types to MIME to provide security services.
Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) has defined several message types that produce new content types to be added to MIME.
In e-mail communication, encryption/decryption is done using a symmetric-key algorithm, but the secret key to encrypt the message is encrypted with the public key of the receiver and is sent with the message.
S/MIME uses public-key certificates signed by the certificate authorities.

Depth-limited search
 Depth-Limited Search is a variation of Depth-First Search (DFS).  It explores nodes in a depth-first manner but only up to a specified depth limit (L).  When the depth limit is reached, the search does not expand further and backtracks.
 It prevents DFS from going too deep into an infinite or very deep path.  If the goal is found within the specified limit, the solution is returned.
 If the goal lies beyond the depth limit, the search returns a cutoff/failure.  It generally uses a LIFO stack or recursion, similar to DFS.

Iterative deepening search
Iterative Deepening Search combines the advantages of Depth-First Search (DFS) and 
Breadth-First Search (BFS). • IDS repeatedly performs Depth-Limited Search (DLS). • It starts with a small depth limit and gradually increases it. 
• First, it searches with Limit = 0, then Limit = 1, then Limit = 2, and so on. 
• Each iteration starts again from the root node. • The process continues until the goal node is found. • Like DFS, it requires relatively low memory. • Like BFS, it can find the shallowest solution when all step costs are equal.

the next move in the search space.

Stochastic Hill Climbing - Algorithm
Step 1: Evaluate the initial state. If it is a goal state, then stop and return success. Otherwise,
make the initial state the current state.
Step 2: Repeat these steps until a solution is found or the current state does not change:
 Select a state that has not yet been applied to the current state.
 Apply the successor function to the current state and generate all the neighbour states.
 Among the generated neighbour states which are better than the current state, choose a
state randomly (or based on some probability function).
 If the chosen state is the goal state, then return success; otherwise, make it the current
state and repeat Step 2.
Step 3: Exit from the function.

slides.text:
Different Regions in the State Space Diagram
• Local maximum: It is a state which is better than its neighbouring states; however, there
exists another state which is better than it (global maximum). The value of the objective
function at this state is higher than its neighbours.
• Global maximum: It is the best possible state in the state space diagram because the
objective function has the highest value at this point.
• Plateau / Flat local maximum: It is a flat region of the state space where neighbouring
states have the same value.
• Ridge: It is a region that is higher than its neighbours but itself has a slope. It is a special
kind of local maximum.
• Current state: The region of the state space diagram where we are currently present
during the search.
• Shoulder: It is a plateau that has an uphill edge.

Problems in Different Regions in Hill Climbing
Hill climbing cannot reach the optimal/best state (global maximum) if it enters any of the
following regions:
Local Maximum: At a local maximum, all neighbouring states have values which are worse
than the current state. Since hill climbing uses a greedy approach, it will not move to the
worse state and terminates itself. The process may end even though a better solution exists.
To overcome local maximum problem: Utilize backtracking technique. Maintain a list of
visited states. If the search reaches an undesirable state, it can backtrack to the previous
configuration and explore a new path.

To overcome plateaus: Make a big jump. Randomly select a state far away from the current 
state. Chances are that we will land in a non-plateau region.

Simulated Annealing
• In metallurgy, annealing is a process in which a material is heated to a high temperature and
then cooled gradually. This allows the material to settle into a stable, low-energy state.
• Simulated Annealing follows a similar idea. Instead of always selecting the best
neighbouring state, the algorithm selects a neighbouring state randomly. • If the new state is better, it is accepted. If the new state is worse, it may still be accepted 
with a certain probability. 
• At a high temperature, the probability of accepting a worse state is higher, which helps the 
algorithm explore different solutions. 
• As the temperature decreases, worse states are accepted less frequently, and the algorithm 
gradually settles toward a good solution.

The generate-and-test strategy is the simplest of all the approaches. It consists of the
following steps:
Algorithm: Generate-and-Test
1. Generate a possible solution. For some problems. this means generating a particular point

2. Test to see if this is actually a solution by comparing the chosen point or the endpoint of
the chosen path to the set of acceptable goal states.
3. If a solution has been found, quit. Otherwise, return to step 1.

Why Do We Need Hypothesis Testing?
• Usually, we cannot study every member of a population. We collect a
sample and use it to make a conclusion about the population.
• Sample results vary naturally from sample to sample. A difference observed
in a sample may simply be due to random chance.
• Hypothesis testing provides a systematic way to decide whether the
observed evidence is strong enough to support or reject a claim.
• Example: A college claims that the average score is 70. If a sample mean is
73, hypothesis testing tells us whether 73 is significantly different from 70.

rects.text: Why Do We Need Hypothesis Testing?

slides.text:
Necessity and Importance
• Makes decisions using sample evidence rather than intuition alone.
• Determines whether an observed difference is statistically significant.
• Helps evaluate scientific and research claims.
• Compares treatments, teaching methods, products, processes, or models.
• Controls the probability of making a Type I error through the significance
level α.
Key idea: hypothesis testing helps distinguish a meaningful signal from
ordinary sampling variation.

So, instead of saying True/False, we use probabilities.

What is a Bayesian Network?
• A Bayesian Network (BN) is a graphical model used to represent uncertain
relationships between different variables.
• It consists of:
Nodes → represent variables.
Directed arrows → represent relationships/dependencies.
Probabilities → represent how likely an event is.

1. Definition
A Markov Decision Process (MDP) is a mathematical model used in Reinforcement Learning to help an agent make 
decisions and choose the best action to achieve a goal.
It learns by interacting with the environment and receiving rewards or penalties.
Example: A robot learns to reach a destination by choosing the correct direction and receiving rewards for 
successful moves.
2. Components of MDP
MDP consists of five main components:
1. Agent: The learner or decision-maker (e.g., robot).
2. Environment: The surroundings in which the agent works.
3. States (S): Different situations in which the agent can be (e.g., robot's current position).
4. Actions (A): Choices available to the agent (e.g., move left, right, forward).
5. Reward (R): Feedback received after performing an action (e.g., +10 for reaching the destination).

Ȳ = ΣY / n = (7 + 8 + 6 + 5 + 6 + 4) / 6 = 36 / 6 = 6

Cov(X,Y) = Σ[(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ)] / n

r = Cov(X,Y) / (σX × σY)

Confusion Matrix
• The confusion matrix is a matrix used to determine the
performance of the classification models for a given set of
test data.
• It can only be determined if the true values for test data are
known.
• The matrix is divided into two dimensions, that are predicted
values and actual values along with the total number of
predictions.
• Predicted values are those values, which are predicted by
the model, and actual values are the true values for the given
observations.
Confusion Matrix

○ True Negative: Model has given prediction No, and the real or actual 
value was also No.
○ True Positive: The model has predicted yes, and the actual value was 
also true.
○ False Negative: The model has predicted no, but the actual value was 
Yes, it is also called as Type-II error.
○ False Positive: The model has predicted Yes, but the actual value was 
No. It is also called a Type-I error.

slides.text:
What Is Logistic Regression?
• A supervised machine-learning algorithm mainly used for classification.
• It estimates the probability that an observation belongs to a class.
• Examples: Pass/Fail, Spam/Not Spam, Fraud/Not Fraud.
For example, suppose a student studies for 6 hours.
Probability of passing = 85%
Probability of failing = 15%
Since the probability of passing is high, the model may predict Pass.
Usually, for binary classification, we use a threshold of 0.5 (50%).
Probability ≥ 0.5 → Pass
Probability < 0.5 → Fail
• Despite the word “regression,” it is commonly used for classification.
• Example: predict whether a student will pass based on study hours.

The Core Idea
• The model calculates a score (Z) from the input features.
• The sigmoid function converts this score into a probability.
• A threshold—often 0.5—turns the probability into a class label.
• If p ≥ 0.5, predict Class 1; otherwise predict Class 0.
Score → Sigmoid → Probability → Class

The Sigmoid Function
• It maps any real-valued score to a value between 0 and 1.
• A value near 0 means low probability of Class 1; near 1 means high probability.
• When z = 0, the sigmoid output is 0.5.
σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ)

Logistic Regression Model
• For one feature: z = b₀ + b₁x.
• For multiple features: z = b₀ + b₁x₁ + b₂x₂ + … + bₙxₙ.
• b₀ is the intercept; b₁, b₂, … are learned coefficients.
• The predicted probability is p = σ(z).
p = 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ)

How the Model Learns
• Start with training examples and known class labels.
• Calculate predicted probabilities using the model.
• Compare predictions with actual labels using a loss function.
A loss function measures how incorrect the predictions are. Logistic Regression commonly 
uses log loss (binary cross-entropy). A lower loss generally indicates better predictions on 
the training examples.
• Adjust coefficients to reduce the loss, commonly using gradient-based optimization.
• Repeat until a stopping condition is reached.

Decision Threshold
• The default threshold is often 0.5, but it is not mandatory.
• A lower threshold predicts more positives and may increase recall and false positives.
Suppose we reduce the threshold from 0.5 to 0.3.
Now, even a probability of 0.40 will be classified as positive.
For example, in disease detection, a lower threshold may help identify more people who 
actually have the disease.
● Advantage: We may detect more actual positive cases (higher recall).
● Disadvantage: We may also incorrectly classify more negative cases as positive (more 
false positives).

Decision Threshold
• A higher threshold predicts fewer positives and may miss more actual positives.
Suppose we increase the threshold from 0.5 to 0.8.
Now, a probability of 0.70 will be classified as negative because it is below 0.8.
● Advantage: The model may produce fewer false positives.
● Disadvantage: It may miss more actual positive cases (more false negatives).
In simple words, the model requires stronger evidence before predicting Class 1.
• Choose a threshold based on the cost of different mistakes.
The best threshold depends on which type of mistake is more serious.
For example, consider a medical test:
● False negative: A sick person is classified as healthy. This could be dangerous.
● False positive: A healthy person is classified as sick. This may lead to unnecessary additional 
testing.
In this case, we may choose a lower threshold to reduce missed cases, while considering the 
additional false positives.

PCA as a Dimensionality Reduction Technique
Dimensionality means the number of features (variables) describing each data record.
When a dataset has many features, some may be correlated or contain overlapping information.
PCA transforms the original features into a smaller set of new features called principal
components.
Principal components are combinations of the original features and are ordered by the amount of
variance they capture.
By keeping only the first few components, we reduce the number of dimensions while retaining as
much variation in the data as possible.
Example: if PC1 explains 80% and PC2 explains 15% of variance, keeping both retains 95% of the
variance while reducing many original features to two components.
PCA may lose information, and the new components can be harder to interpret than the original
features.

extreme cases are called as support vectors, and hence algorithm is termed as Support
Vector Machine.

categorization, etc.

﻿ Arrow function - Core Characteristics Concise Syntax:
Omit the function keyword.
If the body contains only one expression, the curly braces {} and the return keyword can be omitted (implicit return).
If there is exactly one parameter, parentheses () are optional: const square = x => x * x;.

Lexical this Binding: Arrow functions do not have their own this context. Instead, they inherit this from the surrounding (parent) scope. This eliminates the need for .bind(this) or const self = this inside callbacks and event handlers.

Limitations:
Cannot be used as constructors (you cannot call them with new).
Do not have their own arguments object.
Cannot be used as generator functions (no yield keyword).

﻿ React JS React JS is a front-end library developed by Facebook. It is used for handling the view layer for web and mobile apps. 
React JS allows us to create reusable UI components. 
It is currently one of the most popular JavaScript libraries and has a strong foundation and large community behind it. 
React JS is a declarative, efficient, and flexible JavaScript library for building user interfaces. 
It lets you compose complex UIs from small and isolated pieces of code called “components”. 
React JS is a JavaScript library used for building reusable UI components.

﻿ React JS is a library for building composable user interfaces. 
React JS encourages the creation of reusable UI components, which present data that changes over time.

﻿ React Hooks            Hooks are plain JavaScript functions having access to state and lifecycle events of the component in which it is used / applied. In general, hooks starts with use keyword. React comes with a few built-in hooks and allows the creation of custom hooks as well.

Hooks are the new feature introduced in the React 19.2.8 version.

It allows us to use state and other React features without writing a class.

Hooks are the functions which "hook into" React state and lifecycle features from function components. It does not work inside classes.

Hooks are backward-compatible, which means it does not contain any breaking changes.

﻿ The commonly used built-in Hooks include: useState − Used to manipulate state of the component.
useReducer − Advanced version of useState hooks with reducer concept.
useEffect − Used to hook into lifecycle of the component.
useLayoutEffect − Similar to useEffect, but gets triggered synchronously after all DOM mutation or just before the DOM is going to painted on the screen.
useContext − Provides access to the context provider inside a component.
useMemo − Used to return a memorized version of a variable / function, which only changes based on 	supplied  predefined  set  of  dependencies.  This  will  reduce  the  number  of  recomputation  of  expensive 	calculation and improves the performance of the application.
useCallback − returns a memorized version of a callback function, which only changes based on supplied
predefined set of dependencies.
useRef − Provides access to a raw DOM node based on React ref object.

A Single Page Application (SPA) is a web application where the browser loads the main HTML page once, and then React dynamically changes the content when the user navigates.

      ↓
Browser reloads

User clicks About

      ↓
Browser reloads again every navigation may involve loading another page. React SPA

           ↓
              React App
           ↓

       ↓           ↓              ↓
          Home        About      Contact The browser doesn't need to reload the entire page every time.

Introduction to MongoDB
MongoDB is an open-source, NoSQL (Not Only SQL) database used to store and 
manage large amounts of data. It stores data in the form of documents instead of 
rows and columns like traditional relational databases.
MongoDB stores documents in a format called BSON (Binary JSON), which is 
similar to JSON.
Example: In a traditional database, student information is stored in rows and 
columns. In MongoDB, it is stored as documents.
Features of MongoDB
1. NoSQL Database: MongoDB is a non-relational database.
2. Document-Oriented: Data is stored in documents.
3. Flexible Schema: Different documents can have different fields.
4. Scalability: It can handle large amounts of data.
5. High Performance: It provides fast read and write operations.
6. Replication: It maintains multiple copies of data for reliability.
7. Indexing: Indexes help to retrieve data faster.
8. Aggregation: It supports data processing and analysis.
9. JSON-like Format: It stores data in BSON format.
10.Easy Integration: It can be easily connected with Node.js using Mongoose.

1. Introduction to AJAX
AJAX stands for Asynchronous JavaScript and XML. It is a web development 
technique used to create fast, interactive, and dynamic web applications.
AJAX allows web pages to communicate with the web server asynchronously, which 
means that data can be sent to and received from the server without reloading the 
entire web page.
Using AJAX, only a specific part of a webpage can be updated instead of refreshing 
the complete page.
AJAX is not a programming language or a technology by itself. It is a combination of 
several web technologies that work together.
Example:
 When searching on Google, suggestions appear automatically while typing.
 When liking a post on social media, the like count gets updated without 
refreshing the page.
 When submitting a form, the response can be displayed without reloading the 
entire page.

AJAX combines the following technologies:
1. HTML/XHTML: Used to create the structure of web pages.
2. CSS: Used to design and style the webpage.
3. JavaScript: Used to handle user interactions and process responses.
4. DOM (Document Object Model): Used to dynamically modify webpage 
content.
5. XML/JSON: Used to exchange data between the client and server. JSON is 
commonly used in modern AJAX applications.
6. XMLHttpRequest (XHR): Used to send asynchronous HTTP requests to the 
server. The Fetch API is another modern alternative.

entire webpage.
5. Asynchronous Communication: Users can continue interacting with the 
webpage while the server processes a request.
6. Improved Responsiveness: Web applications respond more quickly to user 
actions.
7. Dynamic Content: Content can be updated dynamically without navigating to 
another page.

1. JavaScript Dependency: AJAX requires JavaScript to be enabled in the 
browser.
2. Browser Compatibility: Some browser-specific issues may occur.
3. Security Risks: Improper handling of user input and server responses can 
introduce security vulnerabilities.
4. Debugging Complexity: Asynchronous requests can make debugging more 
difficult.

Rich Internet Applications (RIA)
1. What is RIA?
RIA (Rich Internet Application) is a web application that provides a rich, interactive 
and user-friendly experience similar to desktop applications.
It combines the features of traditional websites with advanced functionality such as 
animations, multimedia, real-time updates and interactive interfaces.
Examples: Gmail, Google Maps, Canva and online banking applications.
2. Features of Rich Internet Applications
1. Rich User Interface: Provides attractive and interactive interfaces.
2. Fast Response: Updates parts of a webpage without reloading the entire 
page.
3. Multimedia Support: Supports audio, video, images and animations.
4. Interactivity: Allows users to interact with application elements.
5. Client-Side Processing: Performs some processing in the user's browser.
6. Real-Time Updates: Displays updated information quickly.
7. Better User Experience: Provides functionality similar to desktop applications.

JavaScript Adds interactivity

 Online Banking: Provides interactive transactions and account updates.
 Canva: Allows users to create and edit designs online.

to create, edit, manage, organize, and publish digital content on a website without 
requiring extensive programming knowledge.
A CMS provides a user-friendly interface through which administrators, content 
creators, and editors can manage website content easily.

business websites, news portals, and e-commerce websites.

images, videos, and documents.
2. Content Editing: Users can modify and update existing website content 
easily.
3. User Management: Provides different user roles such as administrator, 
editor, author, and subscriber.

4. Working of Content Management System
The working of a CMS involves the following steps:
Step 1: User Login
The administrator or content editor logs into the CMS using valid credentials.
Step 2: Content Creation
The user creates new content such as articles, blogs, images, or web pages.
Step 3: Content Editing
The created content can be edited, formatted, and modified using the CMS editor.
Step 4: Content Storage
The content is stored in the CMS database or content repository.
Step 5: Content Management
The administrator manages content by assigning categories, tags, permissions, and 
publishing dates.
Step 6: Content Publishing
The content is published immediately or scheduled for a future date.
Step 7: Website Display
The CMS retrieves the published content and displays it to visitors through the 
website.

 Example: WordPress, Joomla, Drupal.
2. Enterprise Content Management System (ECM)

 Helps store, organize, and retrieve organizational data.

﻿ Principles Resource-Based

resources

﻿ Stateless – The server does not store the client's previous request information. Every request must contain all the information needed to process it. 
Client–Server – The client (frontend) and server (backend) work independently. The client sends requests, and the server processes them and sends responses. 
Uniform Interface – REST follows a standard way of communication. Resources are identified using URLs and manipulated using methods such as GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE. 
Resource-based: Everything is treated as a resource, such as students, users, or products. 
Manipulation of resources: Resources can be created, read, updated, or deleted. 
Self-descriptive messages: Each request/response contains enough information to understand how it should be processed. 
Hypermedia: Responses can contain links to related resources/actions. 
Cacheable – Server responses can be cached when allowed, which reduces server load and improves performance. 
Layered System – A REST system can contain multiple layers, such as security, load balancers, proxies, and servers. The client does not need to know about these intermediate layers. 
Code on Demand – The server may optionally send executable code to the client, such as JavaScript, to extend client functionality.

﻿ RDF:
It is the formal language for describing structured information. The primary goal of RDF is to exchange data on the web while preserving the original meaning of the data. It is a data model that is used to describe resources.
For Example, Physical Things, Abstract Concepts, Numbers and Strings.
RDF allows the processing of information. RDF representation can be in the form of triples and graphs. RDF graph is a directed graph which is used to serve as a description language for data on the world wide web and other electronic networks.
Resources are described using triples. Triples capture the relationship between the subject and the object. Triples have a subject, predicate and an object. Triples are enclosed within angular brackets.
Example: Delhi is capital of India The triple generated from this sentence is:  <Delhi> <capital of> <India>.
, where Delhi is the subject, capital of is the predicate and India is the object. The triples can also be represented in the form of URIs (Uniform Resource Identifier).
Example of URI triple:
<http://www.abc.org/subject/Delhi>
<http://www.abc.org/predicate/capitalOf>
<http://www.abc.org/object/India>.

This non-blocking approach helps Node.js handle many requests efficiently.

﻿ Buffers The Buffer class in Node.js is designed to handle raw binary data.
A temporary memory area that stores binary data
Fixed size: it cannot grow or shrink after creation
Global object: no require() needed
Each element is one byte (a value from 0 to 255)

Why do we need Buffers?
JavaScript originally had no way to handle binary data.
Needed for: file reading, network requests, streams, images, video, encryption
Data arrives in chunks, so Node needs a place to hold each chunk

       When using console.log() to print the Buffer instance, you'll get a chain of values in hexadecimal values.

﻿ Flask       Flask is a lightweight and open-source web framework for Python used to develop web applications and REST APIs. It is called a micro-framework because it provides the essential features needed for web development without forcing a large project structure or many built-in components.

Key Features of Flask
Lightweight: Simple and easy to learn.
Routing: Maps URLs to Python functions using @app.route().
HTTP Methods: Supports GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, etc.
Request and Response: Provides objects for handling client requests and server responses.
Templates: Uses Jinja2 for creating dynamic HTML pages.
Cookies and Sessions: Supports storing user-related information.
Extensions: Additional features such as database connectivity and authentication can be added using extensions.
Development Server: Provides a built-in server for testing applications.

1. Management Information System (MIS)
Definition
A Management Information System (MIS) is an integrated system consisting of people, technology,
processes, and databases that collects, processes, stores, and distributes information to help managers
make better decisions.
Simply,
MIS converts raw data into meaningful information that managers use for planning,
controlling, coordinating and decision-making.
St. Francis Institute of Technology Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia 4

Example
Suppose you own a supermarket.
Every day:
● 200 customers visit.
● Milk sold = 120 packets.
● Bread sold = 80 packets.
● Revenue = ₹35,000.
These numbers alone are data.
When the system prepares a report saying:
"Milk sales increased by 20% compared to yesterday."
This becomes information.
The MIS generates that report.
Famous Definitions
Gordon B. Davis
MIS is an integrated man-machine system that provides information to support operations,
management, and decision-making.
Laudon & Laudon
MIS is a system that collects, processes, stores and disseminates information to support
organizational decision making.
Why Do Organizations Need MIS?
Without MIS:
❌ Decisions become guesses.
❌ Managers waste time.
❌ No proper planning.
❌ Difficult to monitor employees.
❌ No forecasting.
With MIS:

Characteristics of MIS
A good MIS should be:
1. Accurate
Information should be correct.
Wrong information results in poor decisions.
2. Timely
Information should arrive before decisions are made.
Example:
Stock report received after stock finishes is useless.

3. Relevant
Only necessary information should be provided.
A marketing manager doesn't need payroll details every day.
4. Complete

5. Reliable

6. Flexible
Should adapt to changing business needs.
7. Economical

Digital Business
Definition
A digital business uses digital technologies to create value, improve operations, enhance customer
experiences, and generate revenue.
Unlike traditional businesses, digital businesses rely heavily on data, cloud computing, AI, automation,
and online platforms.

Digital Transformation
Definition
Digital transformation is the process of integrating digital technologies into all areas of a business,
fundamentally changing how it operates and delivers value to customers.
It is not just about buying new software—it often requires changes in processes, culture, employee skills,

1. Strategic Information Systems (SIS)
Introduction
Every company uses computers.

Definition

A Transaction Processing System (TPS) is a computerised system that captures, validates,

must reflect the true, current state at every moment.

TPS can process transactions in two main modes. In batch processing, transactions are
collected over a period of time and processed together in one run, which suits high-volume,
non-time-critical work such as monthly payroll or end-of-day bank reconciliation. In real-time

slides.text:
applied at all), and the system maintains detailed audit trails so that every change to the master
data can be traced back to the specific transaction that caused it. This reliability is what allows
every other system - functional area systems, ERP, analytics, and management reporting - to
trust the data flowing up from the TPS layer.
Advantages / Benefits:
• High processing speed and accuracy: Automating routine transactions eliminates
manual data entry errors and processes far more transactions per hour than manual
methods.
• Reliable, auditable records: Every transaction is permanently and consistently
recorded, creating a dependable audit trail for accounting, compliance, and dispute
resolution.
• Foundation for all higher systems: TPS output feeds functional area systems, ERP,
and management reporting, so improving the TPS layer improves the accuracy of every
system built on top of it.
• 24x7 operational capability: Once automated, transaction processing (particularly
online/real-time TPS) can run continuously without requiring constant human
supervision.
• Reduced operating cost per transaction: Automated processing dramatically lowers
the marginal cost of handling each additional transaction compared with manual
processing.
Disadvantages / Limitations:
• High cost of downtime: Because daily operations depend directly on the TPS, any
system outage can halt sales, payments, or production almost immediately.
• Rigid, rule-based processing: A TPS is designed for well-defined, repetitive
transactions and struggles to handle unusual or exceptional cases that fall outside its
programmed rules.

consistent data into ERP, CRM, and reporting systems requires careful system design

Explanation:
Before enterprise-wide integration became common, each department in an organisation often
built or purchased its own dedicated system tailored precisely to its own workflows: a
marketing and sales information system to track leads, campaigns, and sales performance; a
finance and accounting information system to manage the general ledger, accounts payable
and receivable, and financial reporting; a manufacturing and operations information system to
schedule production, monitor machine utilisation, and control quality; and a human resources
information system to manage employee records and payroll.
Each functional area system draws on the same underlying transaction data - a sale recorded by
the TPS is relevant to both the marketing system (as a completed conversion) and the finance
system (as revenue to be recognised) - but transforms that shared data into the specific reports,
dashboards, and decision-support tools that matter to that particular department, rather than
presenting the same raw data to every user regardless of their role.
The major limitation of building functional area systems independently is data fragmentation:
when each department maintains its own separate database, the same customer or product
information can end up duplicated, inconsistently formatted, or simply out of sync between
departments. This exact limitation is the primary reason organisations later moved toward
Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems, which integrate functional area needs around
one shared database rather than many separate ones.
Advantages / Benefits:
• Tailored to departmental needs: Each system is optimised for the specific workflows,
terminology, and reporting requirements of its own department.
• Faster departmental decision-making: Staff get quick access to the specific metrics
and reports relevant to their role without wading through irrelevant enterprise-wide
data.

• Easier to implement individually: A single functional area system is typically smaller
in scope and can be deployed faster and more cheaply than a full enterprise-wide
system.
• Specialised functionality: Departmental systems can include deep, specialised features
