system might not fully support.
• Clear departmental ownership: Each department can manage and customise its own
system according to its own priorities without needing enterprise-wide consensus.
Disadvantages / Limitations:
• Data silos and duplication: The same information (customer, product, or employee
data) can be stored inconsistently across multiple separate systems, leading to
conflicting records.
• Limited cross-department visibility: It becomes difficult to get a single, unified view
of the business when each department's data lives in a separate system.
• Costly integration efforts: Connecting or reconciling data across many independent
functional systems requires additional middleware, manual reconciliation, or custom
integration work.
• Inconsistent reporting: Two departments analysing what should be the same
underlying event can produce different figures if their systems process or define the data
differently.
• Redundant infrastructure costs: Maintaining multiple separate systems (licensing,
hosting, support) is often more expensive overall than one integrated platform.
Examples:
• Example 1: Marketing and sales system. A marketing information system tracks a
campaign's leads and conversions, generating a report on cost per acquisition for the
marketing team's review.
• Example 2: Finance and accounting system. The same sales transaction, once
completed, flows into the finance system, which records the resulting revenue in the
appropriate ledger account for the month's financial statements.
• Example 3: Manufacturing system. A manufacturing information system uses order
data to schedule production runs, allocating machine time and raw materials to meet the
confirmed order quantity by its deadline.
Applications:
• Sales and marketing reporting: Tracking campaign performance, lead conversion,
and sales quotas.
• Financial management: Managing the general ledger, budgets, and financial statement
preparation.

Most ERP systems are organised as a suite of modules that can be implemented together or, in
many cases, adopted incrementally - common modules include Financial Management,
Human Capital Management, Manufacturing and Production, Sales and Distribution,
Procurement, and Inventory and Warehouse Management. Each module is built to handle its
specific business function in depth, while remaining tightly integrated with every other module
through the shared database and a common set of master data (such as one authoritative
customer list or one authoritative product catalogue used by every module).
Implementing ERP is a major undertaking rather than a simple software installation: it
typically requires re-engineering existing business processes to match the ERP system's built￾in best-practice workflows (or, alternatively, customising the ERP software itself), migrating
and cleaning historical data from legacy systems, and extensive staff training, since employees
across every department must learn to work within the new integrated system rather than their
previous, department-specific tools.
Advantages / Benefits:
• Single source of truth: A shared database eliminates data duplication and
inconsistency between departments, since every module reads and writes the same
underlying records.
• Improved cross-department visibility: Management can see a real-time, unified view
of the entire business - sales, inventory, finance, and operations together - rather than
piecing together separate reports.
• Streamlined business processes: Automating handoffs between departments (for
example, sales order automatically triggering procurement) reduces manual re-entry
and processing delays.
• Regulatory and financial compliance support: Centralised, consistent financial data
makes audit trails and statutory reporting significantly easier to produce accurately.
• Scalability for growing organisations: A well-implemented ERP can support an
organisation's growth into new locations, product lines, or business units on the same
core platform.
Disadvantages / Limitations:
• High implementation cost and duration: Large ERP implementations can take many
months or years and require substantial investment in software, consulting, and internal
staff time.
• Significant organisational disruption: Because ERP often requires redesigning
existing business processes, implementation can face strong internal resistance to
change.

sales module automatically reduces available inventory, generates a shipment
instruction in logistics, and creates an invoice in finance, without any manual re-keying
between departments.
• Example 2: Procure-to-pay integration. When inventory falls below a set threshold,
the ERP automatically generates a purchase requisition, which - once approved -
becomes a purchase order that finance can later match against the supplier's invoice for
payment.
• Example 3: Manufacturing resource planning. An ERP's production module uses
current sales orders and inventory data to calculate exactly how much raw material
needs to be procured and scheduled for the next production run.

• Financial management and accounting: Managing the general ledger, accounts
payable/receivable, and financial reporting across the whole organisation.

of materials, and shop-floor operations.
• Supply chain and inventory management: Tracking stock levels, warehouse
operations, and supplier orders in real time.
• Human capital management: Managing recruitment, payroll, and employee records
within the same integrated platform.
• Sales and distribution: Managing customer orders, pricing, and fulfilment as part of
one connected process.

Diagram:
Fig: Supply Chain Management - Material and Information Flow
Explanation:
A supply chain typically spans several linked stages: suppliers who provide raw materials or
components, procurement teams who source and purchase what is needed, manufacturing that
converts inputs into finished goods, warehousing and distribution that store and move
products, retailers who sell to end customers, and finally the customers themselves. SCM
systems coordinate the physical movement of goods forward through this chain while
simultaneously managing the flow of demand and order information backward from customers
toward suppliers, so that production and procurement decisions stay aligned with actual
demand.
Modern SCM relies heavily on visibility and forecasting: by sharing real-time data on
inventory levels, order status, and demand forecasts across every link in the chain,
organisations can reduce the 'bullwhip effect' - a well-documented phenomenon in which
small fluctuations in customer demand become amplified into much larger swings in orders as
they propagate backward through the supply chain, leading to costly overstocking or
stockouts.
Effective SCM systems typically integrate several capabilities: demand planning and
forecasting, procurement and supplier relationship management, inventory optimisation
across multiple warehouse locations, transportation and logistics management, and
increasingly, real-time tracking technologies such as barcode scanning, RFID tagging, and IoT
sensors that give continuous visibility into exactly where goods are at any point in the chain.
Advantages / Benefits:
• Reduced inventory and holding costs: Better demand visibility across the chain lets
organisations hold less safety stock while still meeting customer demand reliably.

• Stronger supplier relationships: Ongoing data sharing and coordination with

• Faster order fulfilment: Coordinated logistics and warehousing reduce the time

• Greater end-to-end visibility: Organisations can track a product's status at every stage,

Disadvantages / Limitations:

inherently difficult.

disruption at a single supplier or port can cascade into delays across the entire chain.

in tracking technology, integration, and data-sharing infrastructure across multiple
organisations.
• Data-sharing and trust barriers: Independent companies within a supply chain may
be reluctant to share sensitive demand or cost data with trading partners.
• Forecasting inaccuracy risk: Poor demand forecasts anywhere in the chain can still
lead to costly overstocking or stockouts even with good coordination systems in place.

triggers a replenishment order to its distribution centre whenever a store's stock of a fast￾selling item falls below a set threshold.

chips, allowing warehouse systems to automatically update inventory records the

An HRIS acts as the single source of truth for all employee-related data throughout the
employment lifecycle, from the moment a candidate applies for a role through onboarding,
ongoing employment, performance reviews, promotions, and eventually exit. Rather than

slides.text:
maintaining separate spreadsheets or systems for recruitment, payroll, and performance

reducing duplicate data entry.
Core HRIS functionality is typically organised into modules that each serve a specific stage or
aspect of the employment relationship. Recruitment and onboarding modules manage job
postings, applicant tracking, and new-hire paperwork. Payroll and benefits modules calculate
salaries, taxes, and deductions, and administer employee benefits enrolment. Performance
management modules track goal-setting, reviews, and ratings over time. Training and
development modules manage learning programmes and track certifications or skill
development. Employee self-service portals let staff view their own payslips, request leave, or
update personal details directly, reducing the administrative burden on HR staff.
Modern HRIS platforms increasingly incorporate analytics capabilities - sometimes called
people analytics or HR analytics - that use the accumulated employee data to identify trends
such as which factors correlate with employee turnover, which recruitment channels produce
the strongest long-term hires, or which teams show early signs of disengagement, turning the
HRIS from a purely administrative record-keeping tool into a genuine strategic decision￾support system for workforce planning.
Advantages / Benefits:
• Centralised, consistent employee data: A single authoritative employee record
eliminates the inconsistencies that arise from maintaining HR data across multiple
disconnected spreadsheets or systems.
• Reduced administrative workload: Automating routine tasks such as payroll
calculation and leave approval frees HR staff to focus on more strategic activities.
• Improved compliance and accuracy: Automated calculation of statutory deductions
and consistent record-keeping reduces the risk of payroll errors and regulatory non￾compliance.
• Employee self-service convenience: Employees can independently check payslips,
request leave, or update details without needing to contact HR directly for routine
matters.
• Data-driven workforce decisions: HR analytics built on accumulated HRIS data help
identify turnover risk, skills gaps, and recruitment effectiveness.
Disadvantages / Limitations:
• Sensitive data privacy risk: An HRIS holds highly sensitive personal, financial, and
health-related employee data, making strong security and access controls essential.
• High implementation and migration cost: Moving historical employee records
accurately from legacy systems into a new HRIS can be a lengthy and costly
undertaking.

approve or reject it, with the approved leave instantly reflected in the payroll
calculation.
• Example 2: Automated payroll run. At the end of each month, the HRIS
automatically calculates each employee's salary, tax deductions, and benefits
contributions based on their attendance and contract details, generating payslips without
manual calculation.
• Example 3: Applicant tracking. A recruiter posts a job opening through the HRIS,
which collects and screens incoming applications, tracks each candidate's progress
through interview stages, and automatically generates onboarding paperwork for the
selected hire.
Applications:
• Recruitment and applicant tracking: Managing job postings, candidate applications,
and hiring workflows.
• Payroll and benefits administration: Calculating salaries, statutory deductions, and
managing employee benefits enrolment.
• Performance management: Tracking goals, reviews, and performance ratings over an
employee's tenure.
• Learning and development tracking: Managing training programmes, certifications,
and skills records.
• Workforce analytics and planning: Analysing HR data to guide staffing, retention,
and organisational planning decisions.

Diagram:
Fig: Knowledge Management Cycle
Explanation:
Knowledge within an organisation is often distinguished into two types: explicit knowledge,
which can be clearly written down, documented, and easily shared (such as a standard
operating procedure or a technical manual), and tacit knowledge, which is harder to articulate
and is typically held in the experience, skills, and judgement of individual employees (such as
a seasoned technician's intuitive understanding of a machine's quirks). A key challenge for
knowledge management is converting valuable tacit knowledge into explicit, shareable form
wherever possible.
Knowledge management is best understood as a continuous cycle rather than a one-time
project. New knowledge is created (through problem-solving, research, or experience),
captured (documented in a usable form, such as a report, wiki page, or recorded discussion),
stored in a shared, searchable repository, shared and disseminated across the organisation
(through training, communities of practice, or simple access to the repository), and applied to
solve new problems or make decisions - and the outcomes and lessons from applying that
knowledge in turn generate new knowledge, feeding back into the start of the cycle.

A KMS typically combines several supporting technologies: a searchable central repository or
knowledge base, collaboration tools such as internal wikis, discussion forums, and shared
workspaces that let employees contribute and refine knowledge together, and increasingly,
intelligent search and recommendation features (sometimes AI-assisted) that surface the most
relevant existing knowledge to an employee at the moment they need it, rather than requiring
them to know exactly what to search for.
Advantages / Benefits:
• Preserves organisational knowledge: Capturing expertise in a shared system reduces
the risk of losing critical know-how when experienced employees leave the
organisation.
• Faster problem-solving: Employees can search existing solutions to similar past
problems instead of solving the same issue repeatedly from scratch.
• Improved consistency and quality: Shared best-practice documentation helps ensure
work is carried out to a consistent standard across teams and locations.
• Accelerated employee onboarding: New employees can learn from a well-organised
knowledge repository far faster than relying solely on informal mentoring.
• Supports innovation: Making existing knowledge easily discoverable helps
employees combine ideas across different areas of the organisation in new ways.
Disadvantages / Limitations:
• Difficult to capture tacit knowledge: Much of the most valuable expertise is hard to
fully document, since experienced employees often cannot easily articulate exactly how
they make certain judgements.
• Requires ongoing employee participation: A knowledge system is only useful if
employees consistently take the time to contribute and update it, which competes with
their regular workload.
• Risk of outdated or inaccurate content: Without active maintenance, a knowledge
repository can accumulate stale or incorrect information that misleads users.
• Information overload: A poorly organised repository with too much unstructured
content can make it harder, not easier, to find genuinely useful knowledge.
• Cultural resistance to sharing: In some organisational cultures, employees may be
reluctant to openly share expertise they see as giving them individual value or job
security.
Examples:
• Example 1: Internal technical wiki. A software company maintains an internal wiki
where engineers document solutions to tricky bugs, letting future engineers search and
resolve similar issues without repeating the same investigation.

Fig: AI Layer Built on Core Enterprise Systems
Explanation:
Traditional enterprise systems are primarily designed to capture and process transactional data
accurately - recording what has already happened. AI-enabled enterprise systems build an
additional intelligence layer on top of this transactional foundation, applying techniques such
as predictive analytics, natural language processing, and machine learning models to the
accumulated data to generate forward-looking insight rather than only historical record￾keeping.
This AI layer typically draws on the large volumes of transactional data already flowing
through core systems like ERP, CRM, SCM, and HRIS, and applies it to specific business
problems: predicting which machines are likely to fail before they actually do (predictive
maintenance), forecasting future product demand more accurately than simple historical
averages, automatically extracting and processing information from unstructured documents
such as invoices or contracts, and automating repetitive, rule-based digital tasks through
robotic process automation (RPA).
The result of this AI layer is delivered back to business users not as raw data but as actionable
insights and, in many cases, automated decisions or workflows - a forecast that automatically
adjusts a purchase order, an anomaly detection alert that flags a suspicious transaction for
review, or a chatbot that resolves a routine customer query without human involvement. This
shifts the role of enterprise systems from purely operational record-keeping toward active
decision support and, in some cases, autonomous action.

• Improved decision-making speed and quality: AI-generated forecasts and
recommendations help managers make faster, more informed decisions than manual
analysis of raw historical data alone.
• Proactive rather than reactive operations: Predictive capabilities such as predictive
maintenance let organisations act before a problem occurs rather than only responding
after the fact.
• Automation of repetitive work: AI-driven automation (such as RPA) frees employees
from repetitive digital tasks to focus on higher-value work.
• Greater accuracy at scale: Machine learning models can analyse far more data, and
identify subtler patterns, than manual analysis could realistically achieve.
• Continuously improving performance: Many AI models improve their accuracy over
time as more data accumulates, unlike static, rule-based systems.
Disadvantages / Limitations:
• Requires large volumes of quality data: AI models are only as good as the data they
are trained on; poor-quality or biased underlying enterprise data leads to poor or unfair
predictions.
• High implementation complexity and cost: Building and integrating AI capabilities
into existing enterprise systems requires specialised skills and significant investment.
• Lack of transparency ('black box' models): Some AI models make it difficult to fully
explain why a specific prediction or recommendation was made, which can be a
problem for high-stakes or regulated decisions.
• Risk of over-automation: Automating decisions without adequate human oversight
can lead to costly errors when the AI encounters situations it was not trained to handle
correctly.
• Ongoing model maintenance burden: AI models can degrade in accuracy over time as
business conditions change, requiring continuous monitoring and retraining.
Examples:
• Example 1: Predictive maintenance in manufacturing. Sensors on factory equipment
feed data into an AI model that predicts an imminent bearing failure, allowing
maintenance to be scheduled before the machine actually breaks down and halts
production.
• Example 2: AI-driven demand forecasting. A retailer's ERP uses machine learning to
forecast next month's demand for a product far more accurately than a simple average of
past sales, accounting for seasonality, promotions, and external trends.
• Example 3: Automated invoice processing. An AI-enabled finance system
automatically reads incoming supplier invoices, extracts the relevant data using optical
character recognition and NLP, and matches it against the corresponding purchase order
without manual data entry.

Definition:
The System Development Life Cycle (SDLC) is a structured, phased methodology for
planning, creating, testing, and deploying an information system, breaking the overall
development effort into a series of well-defined stages - each with its own specific activities
and deliverables - to ensure that a system is built systematically, meets requirements, and can
be maintained reliably over its lifetime.

do. Design translates those requirements into a technical blueprint, covering the system's

The classic SDLC divides system development into a sequence of phases. Planning establishes
the project's scope, objectives, feasibility, and resource requirements. Analysis gathers and
documents detailed requirements from stakeholders, defining exactly what the system must
do. Design translates those requirements into a technical blueprint, covering the system's

slides.text:
architecture, database structure, and user interface. Implementation (or development) is where
the actual code is written based on the design. Testing verifies that the system works correctly
and meets requirements, catching defects before release. Deployment releases the finished
system into the live production environment for actual use. Maintenance covers the ongoing
period after deployment, during which bugs are fixed, minor enhancements are made, and the
system is kept running correctly.
Each phase in the SDLC produces a specific, tangible deliverable that becomes the input to the
next phase - for example, the analysis phase produces a requirements document that the design
phase then uses as its starting point - which is what gives the SDLC its structured, traceable
nature and makes it easier to track project progress and assign accountability at each stage.
Although often illustrated as a straight, one-directional sequence (sometimes called the
'waterfall' approach when phases strictly follow one another without revisiting earlier stages),
in practice the maintenance phase commonly reveals new requirements or issues that feed
directly back into the planning phase for the system's next release or version, making the
overall SDLC a repeating cycle across a system's full multi-year lifetime rather than a single
one-off project.
Advantages / Benefits:
• Structured and predictable process: Breaking development into clear phases makes it
easier to plan timelines, budgets, and resource allocation accurately.
• Clear documentation at every stage: Each phase's deliverables create a documented
trail that makes the system easier to understand, audit, and maintain later.
• Easier progress tracking: Well-defined phase boundaries make it straightforward for
management to monitor whether a project is on schedule.
• Reduced risk of missed requirements: A dedicated analysis phase ensures
requirements are captured and agreed upon before significant development effort is
invested.
• Facilitates quality assurance: A dedicated testing phase built into the process helps
catch defects before they reach end users in production.
Disadvantages / Limitations:
• Inflexibility to changing requirements: In its traditional (waterfall-style) form, the
SDLC makes it costly and disruptive to accommodate requirement changes discovered
after the analysis phase has concluded.
• Delayed delivery of working software: Users may not see or be able to use any part of
the system until very late in the process, increasing the risk of building the wrong thing.
• Time-consuming for large projects: Completing every phase thoroughly for a large
system can take a long time, during which business needs may have already changed.
• High dependency on upfront documentation quality: If early requirements or design
documents are flawed or incomplete, those flaws propagate through every subsequent
phase.

• Government and public-sector IT projects: Managing large, accountable technology
projects with clearly defined phases and deliverables.
• Academic and training contexts: Teaching structured software engineering practice as
the foundation before introducing more flexible modern methodologies.

repeated cycles (sprints) involving continuous collaboration with stakeholders and the
flexibility to adapt to changing requirements, while DevOps extends this philosophy by
combining software development and IT operations into one continuous, automated pipeline
that takes code from development through to release, deployment, and live monitoring.

Explanation:
Agile emerged as a direct response to the rigidity of traditional, sequential development
approaches like the classic SDLC waterfall model. Instead of trying to fully define all
requirements upfront and delivering one large system at the very end of a long project, Agile
breaks work into short iterations (commonly one to four weeks, called sprints), each of which
produces a small, working increment of the system that stakeholders can review and provide
feedback on immediately - allowing the team to adapt direction continuously rather than
discovering misalignment only at the very end.
Within each Agile sprint, a team typically cycles through planning the sprint's goals, writing
code, and testing the resulting increment, repeating this loop sprint after sprint until the product
is complete or the team decides to stop. This tight feedback loop, combined with close,
ongoing collaboration between developers and business stakeholders, is what makes Agile far
more adaptable to changing requirements than traditional sequential approaches.
DevOps takes the same underlying philosophy of continuous, iterative improvement and
extends it beyond development into the operational side of running software in production.
Where Agile focuses mainly on the plan-code-build-test cycle, DevOps adds release,
deployment, operation, and monitoring into the same continuous loop, typically automated
through practices such as continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines.

feedback directly back into the next planning cycle, so that operational lessons continuously

Fig: Cloud ERP - Multi-Tenant SaaS Architecture
Explanation:
In the traditional, on-premise ERP model, an organisation purchases ERP software licences
and then installs, hosts, and maintains the entire system on its own servers - requiring
significant upfront capital investment in hardware, as well as an internal IT team to manage
upgrades, security patches, and infrastructure. In the cloud ERP model, the vendor instead
hosts the application, database, and infrastructure centrally, and organisations access it as a
service, typically paying a recurring subscription fee based on usage or number of users.
Most cloud ERP platforms use a multi-tenant architecture, meaning that a single instance of
the underlying application and infrastructure serves many different client organisations
(tenants) simultaneously, with each tenant's data kept logically separated and secure from
every other tenant. This design lets the vendor apply software updates, security patches, and
new features to every customer at once, rather than each organisation needing to independently
plan and execute its own upgrade project.
Users access a cloud ERP system through a standard web browser or mobile application,
connecting over the internet to the vendor's infrastructure - which handles the application
logic, the shared database, and the underlying servers and storage. This shifts the responsibility
for infrastructure capacity planning, uptime, disaster recovery, and much of the day-to-day
system security away from the customer organisation and onto the cloud ERP vendor.
Advantages / Benefits:
• Lower upfront investment: Organisations avoid large capital expenditure on servers
and infrastructure, paying instead through predictable, recurring subscription fees.

• Faster deployment: Since the vendor already hosts the core infrastructure, a cloud ERP
can typically be implemented and rolled out faster than a comparable on-premise
system.
• Automatic updates and maintenance: The vendor handles software updates, security

• Access from anywhere: Because the system is accessed over the internet, employees

distributed teams.
• Easier scalability: Organisations can typically scale their usage (adding users or

hardware investment to scale.
Disadvantages / Limitations:
• Ongoing dependency on internet connectivity: Since the system is hosted remotely, a
loss of internet access can prevent employees from using the ERP entirely.
• Recurring cost accumulation: While avoiding large upfront costs, subscription fees
accumulate over time and can exceed the total cost of on-premise ownership over a long
enough period.
• Less control over customisation: Multi-tenant cloud architectures often limit how
deeply an individual organisation can customise the system compared with a dedicated
on-premise deployment.
• Data security and residency concerns: Storing sensitive business data on a third-party
vendor's infrastructure raises questions about data protection, jurisdiction, and
regulatory compliance that must be carefully evaluated.
• Vendor dependency risk: Switching cloud ERP vendors later can be difficult and
costly, since a business's data and workflows become deeply tied to a specific vendor's
platform.

• Example 1: A growing retailer adopting cloud ERP. A mid-sized retail chain adopts
a cloud ERP system to manage finance and inventory across multiple stores without
having to invest in its own data centre, paying a monthly subscription based on the
number of users.
• Example 2: Remote access during expansion. A company expanding into a new
country lets its new regional team access the same cloud ERP instance immediately over
the internet, without needing to set up new local servers.
• Example 3: Automatic feature rollout. A cloud ERP vendor releases a new AI￾powered forecasting feature that becomes automatically available to all subscribing
customers at once, without any of them needing to manually install an upgrade.

slides.text:
Explanation:
SAP's ERP systems are organised into distinct functional modules that map closely to core
business processes, including SAP FI (Financial Accounting) for managing the general ledger
and financial reporting, SAP MM (Materials Management) for procurement and inventory,
SAP SD (Sales and Distribution) for order and sales processing, SAP HCM (Human Capital
Management) for HR functions, and SAP PP (Production Planning) for manufacturing
scheduling - all sharing a single, tightly integrated central database, so that a transaction in one
module is instantly reflected across every other relevant module.
A defining feature of SAP's more recent ERP generation, S/4HANA, is its use of an in-memory
database architecture: rather than storing and retrieving data primarily from slower disk-based
storage, HANA holds much of the active dataset directly in fast computer memory,
dramatically accelerating the complex real-time reporting and analytics that large
organisations rely on for day-to-day decision-making.
SAP implementations at large multinational organisations are typically substantial, multi-year
projects involving extensive business-process re-engineering, data migration from legacy
systems, and specialist SAP consulting expertise, reflecting both the depth of functionality
SAP offers and the scale of organisational change required to adopt it successfully across a
large, complex enterprise.
Advantages / Benefits:
• Deep, mature functionality: Decades of development have given SAP extremely
comprehensive coverage of complex business processes across virtually every industry.
• Strong integration across modules: SAP's tightly connected modules provide a
genuinely unified view of finance, operations, and HR for large, complex organisations.
• High-performance real-time analytics: The HANA in-memory database enables fast
reporting and analytics even on very large datasets.
• Large global support ecosystem: A vast network of SAP-certified consultants,
partners, and specialists makes it easier to find implementation and support expertise
worldwide.
• Strong industry-specific solutions: SAP offers pre-configured industry variants
tailored to sectors such as manufacturing, retail, and utilities.
Disadvantages / Limitations:
• Very high implementation cost and complexity: Large SAP deployments are among
the most expensive and time-consuming ERP implementations in the industry.
• Steep learning curve: SAP's depth and complexity mean staff often require significant
training to use the system effectively.
• Heavy reliance on specialist consultants: Successful implementation and
customisation typically require expensive, specialised SAP consulting expertise.
• Rigid upgrade cycles: Moving between major SAP versions (such as older ECC
systems to S/4HANA) can itself be a substantial, disruptive project.

AI-integrated enterprise applications are real-world business systems that have moved beyond

slides.text:
Both SAP and Oracle, alongside other major enterprise vendors, have progressively embedded
AI capabilities directly into their core ERP and CRM offerings rather than positioning AI as a
separate, optional add-on product. This reflects a broader industry shift: modern enterprise
applications are increasingly expected not just to record what has already happened, but to
actively predict what is likely to happen next and, in many cases, take or recommend action
automatically.
Concrete examples of this integration include predictive maintenance capabilities that analyse
sensor and equipment data to warn of likely failures before they occur, demand forecasting
models that improve inventory and production planning accuracy beyond simple historical
averages, AI-powered chatbots and virtual assistants embedded directly within ERP or CRM
interfaces to help employees and customers complete tasks through natural conversation, and
robotic process automation that handles repetitive digital tasks such as invoice matching or
data entry without human intervention.
Studying these real-world case studies shows that successfully embedding AI into enterprise
applications is not simply a matter of adding a new software feature: it requires a solid
underlying data foundation from well-integrated core systems (since AI models depend on
large volumes of accurate transactional data), careful change management so that employees
trust and adopt AI-driven recommendations, and clear governance over when a system should
recommend an action to a human versus taking that action automatically.
Advantages / Benefits:
• Demonstrates a clear evolution path for enterprise systems: These case studies show
organisations concretely how traditional ERP/CRM platforms are evolving toward
genuinely intelligent, predictive systems.
• Provides measurable business impact evidence: Real deployments of predictive
maintenance, forecasting, and automation give concrete, quantifiable examples of AI's
return on investment in enterprise settings.
• Highlights practical implementation lessons: Studying real cases surfaces the data
quality, integration, and change-management challenges that any AI adoption effort
needs to plan for.
• Shows vendor-neutral patterns: Comparing how different major vendors have
approached embedding AI reveals common patterns and best practices applicable across
platforms.
• Builds confidence for adoption: Seeing successful, real-world examples helps other
organisations build the internal business case for investing in similar AI-enabled
capabilities.
Disadvantages / Limitations:
• Vendor-reported results may be optimistic: Case studies published by vendors
themselves may emphasise successes and understate the difficulties encountered during
implementation.

What is Data Management?
Definition: Data management is the process of collecting, storing, 
organizing, protecting, and maintaining an organization's data so that it 
is accurate, available, and usable for business operations and decision￾making.
• Good data management ensures data quality, security, accessibility, 
and compliance with regulations (e.g., data privacy laws).
• Poor data management leads to duplicate, inconsistent, or unreliable 
data, which weakens business decisions.
Database Management System (DBMS)
• Definition: A Database Management System (DBMS) is software 
that allows organizations to create, store, organize, retrieve, and 
manage data in an efficient, secure, and reliable way.
• A DBMS acts as an interface between the user/application and the 
physical database, so users do not need to know how data is actually 
stored on disk.
• It supports data creation, insertion, updation, deletion, and querying 
using languages such as SQL (Structured Query Language).
• Key functions of a DBMS: 
◦ Data storage, retrieval, and update.
◦ Enforcing data integrity and consistency rules (constraints, keys, 
relationships).
◦ Providing security through authentication, authorization, and 
access control.
◦ Supporting concurrent multi-user access without conflicts 
(concurrency control).

ACID Properties of a DBMS Transaction
• Atomicity: A transaction is treated as a single, indivisible unit — it 
either completes fully or not at all.
• Consistency: A transaction takes the database from one valid state 
to another, preserving all defined rules.
• Isolation: Concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other; 
each executes as if it were alone.
• Durability: Once a transaction is committed, its changes are 
permanent, even after a system failure.

According to Bill Inmon, a data warehouse has four defining 
characteristics:
• Subject-oriented – organized around key business subjects such as 
sales, customers, or products rather than around applications.
• Integrated – data from different sources is made consistent in 
naming, format, and units.
• Time-variant – data is stored with a time dimension, allowing trend 
and historical analysis.
• Non-volatile – once data enters the warehouse, it is not changed or 
deleted; it is only added to.

reducing redundancy but increasing query complexity.

• Data marts are faster to build and query than a full data warehouse

allowing the sales team to analyze performance quickly without

• Volume: The sheer scale of data generated every day — from 
terabytes to zettabytes — by social media, sensors, transactions, and 
devices.
• Velocity: The speed at which new data is generated and must be 
processed, often in real time (e.g., stock trades, IoT sensor streams, 
UPI transactions).
• Variety: Data exists in structured (tables), semi-structured (XML, 
JSON), and unstructured (images, video, social posts) forms.
• Veracity: The trustworthiness, accuracy, and quality of the data —
noisy, incomplete, or biased data reduces the value of analysis.
• Value: The ultimate business usefulness that can be extracted from 
the data through analytics — data is only "big" data if it can be 
turned into insight.
Big Data Technologies
• Hadoop: An open-source framework that allows distributed storage 
(HDFS) and processing (MapReduce) of very large datasets across 
clusters of commodity computers.
• Apache Spark: An in-memory, distributed data-processing engine 
that is significantly faster than traditional MapReduce for iterative 
analytics and machine learning.
• NoSQL databases: Databases such as MongoDB and Cassandra 
designed to handle unstructured or semi-structured Big Data at scale.
Case studies: Amazon analyzes clickstream and purchase data at
massive scale to power personalized product recommendations; Netflix 
processes viewing data across hundreds of millions of users worldwide 
to personalize content and design new shows; Indian digital enterprises 
such as UPI-based payment platforms process billions of real-time 
transactions daily, requiring high-velocity Big Data infrastructure.

decisions instead of relying on intuition alone.

Fig 2.9: Types of Business Analytics — Descriptive, Diagnostic, 
Predictive, and Prescriptive.
• Descriptive analytics: Summarizes historical data to explain "what 
happened" (e.g., last quarter's sales report).
• Diagnostic analytics: Examines data to understand "why it 
happened" (e.g., root-cause analysis of a sales drop).
• Predictive analytics: Uses statistical models and machine learning 
on historical data to forecast "what is likely to happen" (e.g., 
predicting customer churn or demand).
• Prescriptive analytics: Recommends specific actions — "what 
should be done" — often using optimization and AI techniques (e.g., 
dynamic pricing recommendations).
Common predictive-analytics techniques include regression analysis, 
decision trees, time-series forecasting, and neural networks. These are 
widely used for demand forecasting, credit-risk scoring, churn 
prediction, and predictive maintenance in manufacturing.

Multidimensional data model is provided that is intuitively analytical and easy to use.

Transparency:

Accessibility:

Generic Dimensionality:

operational capabilities. Have one logical structure for all dimensions.

created and loaded that optimizes sparse matrix handling.

1. Data Storage

2. Data Retrieval
It allows users to find required information quickly.
Example:

3. Data Modification
Users can update existing information.

6. Data Integrity

11. Characteristics of Big Data — The 5 Vs
A very important concept for exams is the 5 Vs of Big Data.
1. Volume
Means the huge amount of data.
Example
Facebook stores enormous amounts of photos, videos and messages.
Volume = How much data?
2. Velocity
Means the speed at which data is generated and processed.
Example
Stock market prices change every second.

3. Variety
Means the different types and formats of data.
Examples:
● Text

● Audio
● Numbers
● Social media posts

4. Veracity

5. Value

What is Information Security?
Definition: Information security is the practice of protecting information 
and information systems from unauthorized access, use, disclosure, 
disruption, modification, or destruction, in order to preserve their value 
to the organization.
• Information security applies to data in all forms — digital, printed, 
or spoken — and covers people, processes, and technology.
• It is a continuous process, not a one-time project, because threats 
and technology keep evolving.
The CIA Triad

goals of information security:

• Confidentiality: Ensures that information is accessible only to 
authorized individuals and is protected from unauthorized disclosure 
(e.g., encryption, access controls).
• Integrity: Ensures that data is accurate, complete, and has not been 
altered by unauthorized parties (e.g., checksums, digital signatures, 
version control).
• Availability: Ensures that information and systems are accessible to 
authorized users whenever needed (e.g., redundancy, backups, 
disaster recovery).
Example: A hospital's patient database must keep records confidential 
(only doctors can view them), accurate (integrity of diagnosis data), and 
available (accessible during emergencies).
Information Security Threats
• Threat: Any circumstance or event with the potential to cause harm 
to an information system (e.g., a hacker, a virus, a natural disaster).
• Vulnerability: A weakness in a system, process, or control that can 
be exploited by a threat (e.g., outdated software, weak passwords).
• Risk: The potential for loss or damage when a threat exploits a 
vulnerability; often expressed as Risk = Threat × Vulnerability × 
Impact.

Fig 3.4: Symmetric encryption (same key for encryption/decryption) vs 
Asymmetric encryption (public/private key pair).
• Symmetric encryption: Uses the same secret key for both 
encryption and decryption. It is fast but requires the key to be shared 
securely beforehand. Example: AES, DES.
• Asymmetric encryption: Uses a mathematically linked pair of keys 
— a public key (to encrypt) and a private key (to decrypt). It solves 
the key-sharing problem but is slower. Example: RSA.
• Digital signatures: Use asymmetric cryptography to verify the 
authenticity and integrity of a message or document.

Information Security Policies
Definition: A security policy is a formal, documented set of rules and 
guidelines that defines how an organization protects its information 
assets and expects employees to behave regarding security.
• Acceptable Use Policy (AUP): Defines permitted and prohibited 
uses of company IT resources, such as email and internet access.
• Password Policy: Sets rules for password length, complexity, 
expiry, and reuse to reduce the risk of compromise.
• Data Classification Policy: Categorizes data (e.g., Public, Internal, 
Confidential, Restricted) so appropriate protection levels can be 
applied.
• Backup and Disaster Recovery Policy: Defines how frequently 
data is backed up and how systems will be restored after a disruptive 
event.
• Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) Policy: Governs the security 
requirements for personal devices used to access organizational data.

• Preparation: Building policies, tools, and trained teams before an

• Identification: Detecting and confirming that a security incident has

• Containment: Limiting the spread and impact of the incident (short￾term and long-term containment).

Cybersecurity Awareness and Training
Why it matters: Studies consistently show that human error — clicking 
a phishing link, using a weak password, misconfiguring a system — is 
involved in the majority of security breaches, making people as 
important a layer of defense as technology.
• Security awareness training: Regular training programs that teach 
employees to recognize phishing attempts, follow password hygiene, 
and report suspicious activity promptly.
• Simulated phishing exercises: Organizations send mock phishing 
emails to employees to measure susceptibility and reinforce safe 
behavior through immediate feedback.
• Security champions programs: Nominating security-conscious 
employees within each department to promote good practices and 
act as a first point of contact for concerns.
• Onboarding and role-based training: New employees and those in 
sensitive roles (finance, IT admin) receive targeted training on the 
specific risks relevant to their responsibilities.

Privacy: The right of individuals to control how their personal 
information is collected, used, stored, and shared.
• Data collection concerns: Organizations collect vast amounts of 
personal data (browsing history, location, purchase behavior), often 
without users fully understanding how it will be used.
• Informed consent: Ethical systems should clearly inform users 
what data is collected and obtain explicit permission before use.
• Data ownership: Questions of who truly owns personal data — the 
individual, the company that collects it, or both.
• Surveillance: Increasing use of tracking technologies (cookies, 
facial recognition, location tracking) raises concerns about excessive 
monitoring of individuals.
• Digital divide: Unequal access to technology and information can 
create ethical concerns about fairness and inclusion.
• Intellectual property: Ethical and legal issues around unauthorized 
use, copying, or distribution of digital content and software.
Key regulations: Many countries have enacted data-protection laws —
for example, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in the 
European Union and India's Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) 
Act — that give individuals rights over their personal data and place 
obligations on organizations that collect it.

Explainable AI (XAI)
Definition: Explainable AI refers to methods and techniques that make 
the outputs and decision-making process of AI systems understandable 
to humans, in contrast to opaque "black-box" models.
Fig 3.7: A black-box AI model gives a decision with no explanation, 
while an Explainable AI (XAI) model justifies its output.
• XAI is especially important in high-stakes domains such as banking 
(loan rejection reasons), healthcare (diagnosis justification), and 
criminal justice (risk-assessment scoring).
• Techniques include feature-importance scores, decision trees/rule￾based models (naturally interpretable), and post-hoc explanation 
methods such as LIME and SHAP that approximate why a complex 
model made a specific prediction.
• Explainability builds user trust, supports regulatory compliance, and 
helps developers debug and improve models.

• Diverse and representative training data: Ensuring datasets

• Human-in-the-loop review: Keeping a human reviewer in the

automating them.
AI Governance and Regulation
• EU Artificial Intelligence Act: A landmark regulation that 
classifies AI systems by risk level (unacceptable, high, limited, 
minimal) and imposes stricter obligations on high-risk applications 
such as biometric identification and critical infrastructure.
• India's approach to AI governance: India has emphasized a 
principle-based, pro-innovation approach, with government 
advisories on responsible AI use and ongoing policy discussions 
(e.g., under NITI Aayog's Responsible AI framework) rather than a 
single comprehensive AI law.
• Organizational AI governance: Many companies now set up 
internal AI ethics boards or review committees to evaluate high-risk 
AI projects before deployment.
Common AI Ethics Challenges
• Algorithmic bias: AI models trained on historical data can inherit 
and amplify existing societal biases (e.g., a facial recognition system 
performing poorly for certain skin tones).
• Job displacement: Automation and AI adoption can displace human 
workers, raising socio-economic concerns.

• Insider threats: Several notable incidents have involved current or

Common lesson across these case studies: strong technical controls must 
be paired with employee awareness training, timely patching, vendor 
risk assessment, and a well-rehearsed incident response plan, since 
human error and third-party risk remain among the leading causes of 
breaches.
Emerging Technology Security Considerations
• Internet of Things (IoT) security: Billions of connected devices 
(smart cameras, sensors, wearables) often ship with weak default 
credentials and infrequent updates, making them attractive targets 
for building large-scale botnets.
• Cloud security: Shifting data and applications to cloud platforms 
introduces a shared-responsibility model, where the cloud provider 
secures the underlying infrastructure while the customer remains 
responsible for securing their own data, configurations, and access 
controls.
• Blockchain and security: Blockchain's decentralized, tamper￾evident ledger can enhance data integrity and transparency, but 
smart-contract bugs and private-key theft remain significant risk 
areas.
• Quantum computing implications: Future large-scale quantum 
computers could theoretically break widely used asymmetric 
encryption (e.g., RSA), motivating early research into "post￾quantum cryptography."

Definition: Digital governance refers to the frameworks, policies, and 
processes by which an organization directs and controls its use of digital 
technology, data, and AI to ensure they are secure, ethical, and aligned 
with business and regulatory requirements.
Fig 3.7: A layered Digital Governance framework, from leadership 
down to monitoring.
• Governance bodies: Boards, Chief Information Officers (CIOs), 
and Chief Information Security Officers (CISOs) set the strategic 
direction and accountability for digital risk.
• Policies and standards: Formal rules covering data handling, 
acceptable use, security requirements, and responsible AI use.
• Compliance and risk management: Ensuring adherence to laws 
and regulations (e.g., data-protection acts) through audits and risk 
assessments.
• Monitoring and reporting: Continuously tracking security metrics, 
incidents, and policy effectiveness, and reporting to leadership for 
improvement.

Chapter 3: Cybersecurity, Ethics and 
Emerging Technologies
These notes are based on Module 3 of your syllabus and cover:
● Information Security and Security Threats
● Cyber-attacks and Security Controls
● Privacy and Ethical Issues in Information Systems
● AI Ethics and Responsible AI
● Cybersecurity Incidents and Digital Governance
3.1 Information Security and Security 
Threats
1. Meaning of Information Security
Information Security means protecting information and information systems from:
● Unauthorized access
● Unauthorized use
● Unauthorized modification
● Disclosure of confidential information
● Destruction or loss of information
● Disruption of information systems 
In simple words:
Information security means ensuring that the right information is available to 
the right people, at the right time, and is protected from unauthorized people 
and harmful activities.

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
Example
Consider a college's student database. 
It contains:
● Student names
● Marks
● Attendance
● Phone numbers
● Fee information
The database should be protected so that:
● Only authorized people can access it.
● Nobody can secretly change marks.
● The information is not deleted accidentally.
● Sensitive information is not leaked.
All these protections together are part of Information Security.
2. CIA Triad
The three fundamental goals of information security are:
1. Confidentiality
2. Integrity
3. Availability
Together, they are called the CIA Triad.
CIA here does not refer to the intelligence agency. It stands for 
Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability.
2.1 Confidentiality
Confidentiality means protecting information from unauthorized access or disclosure. 
Only authorized people should be able to see sensitive information.

rects.text: Only authorized people should be able to see sensitive information.

slides.text:
SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
Example
A student's examination marks should be accessible to:
● The student
● Authorized teachers
● The examination department
An unknown person should not be able to access or download everyone's marks.
Methods used to maintain confidentiality
● Passwords
● Encryption
● Authentication
● Access control
● Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
Simple Example
Your WhatsApp messages should only be visible to you and the intended recipient. If a stranger 
reads them without permission, confidentiality has been violated.
2.2 Integrity
Integrity means ensuring that information remains:
● Accurate
● Complete
● Correct
● Unchanged unless modified by an authorized person
Example
Suppose a student originally scores 75 marks.
If someone illegally changes the marks from 75 to 95, the integrity of the data has been 
compromised.
Similarly, if a bank account balance is ₹10,000 and someone changes it to ₹1,00,000 without 
authorization, this is an integrity violation.
Methods used to maintain integrity

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
● Access controls
● Digital signatures
● Hashing
● Audit trails
● Backups
2.3 Availability
Availability means ensuring that information and systems are accessible when authorized
users need them.
Example
During online examination registration, thousands of students may access the university 
website.
If the website crashes and students cannot register, the availability of the system has been 
affected.
Methods used to maintain availability
● Regular system maintenance
● Data backups
● Redundant servers
● Disaster recovery systems
● Protection against Denial-of-Service attacks
2.4 Understanding the CIA Triad Through One Example
Imagine an online banking system:
Security Goal Meaning Example
Confidentiality Only authorized people can see 
information
Only the account holder can view their 
bank balance
Integrity Information remains correct Nobody can illegally change the 
account balance

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
Availability System is available when needed Customers can access online banking
when required
3. Security Threat
A security threat is any potential danger that can harm an information system or its data. 
A threat may come from:
● Hackers
● Malicious software
● Employees
● Human mistakes
● System failures
● Natural disasters
Example
A hacker attempting to steal customer passwords is a security threat.
However, even an employee accidentally deleting an important database can become a threat 
to information security.
4. Types of Security Threats
4.1 Malware
Malware stands for Malicious Software.
It is software designed to harm, disrupt, steal information from, or gain unauthorized access to a 
computer system.
Common types include:
● Virus
● Worm
● Trojan Horse
● Ransomware

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
● Spyware
Virus
A computer virus attaches itself to a file or program and can spread when that file is executed.
Example
A person downloads an infected file. When they open it, the virus infects other files on the 
computer.
Worm
A worm is malware that can automatically spread from one computer to another, usually 
through networks.
Unlike many viruses, a worm does not necessarily require a user to open an infected file to 
spread.
Trojan Horse
A Trojan Horse appears to be legitimate software but secretly performs harmful activities.
Example
A user downloads a fake game that appears normal. In the background, it steals passwords 
from the computer.
Ransomware
Ransomware is malware that locks or encrypts a victim's data and demands money for 
restoring access.
Example
A company opens an infected email attachment. Its important files become inaccessible, and 
the attackers demand payment to restore them.

slides.text:
SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
Spyware
Spyware secretly collects information about a user. 
It may collect:
● Browsing activity
● Passwords
● Personal information
● Other sensitive data
4.2 Phishing
Phishing is a cyber-attack in which attackers pretend to be a trusted person or organization to 
trick users into revealing sensitive information.
The attacker may send:
● Fake emails
● Fake messages
● Fake websites
Example
You receive an email saying:
"Your bank account will be blocked. Click here immediately to verify your account."
The link takes you to a fake website that looks like the real bank website. When you enter your 
username and password, the attacker steals them.
This is phishing.
4.3 Social Engineering
Social engineering means manipulating people into revealing confidential information or 
performing actions that help an attacker.
Instead of directly attacking a computer, the attacker targets human behaviour.

username and password, the attacker steals them.
performing actions that help an attacker.

slides.text:
SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
Example
An attacker calls an employee and says:
"Hello, I am from the IT department. We need your password to fix a technical 
problem."
If the employee believes the attacker and provides the password, the attack succeeds.
Important idea:
In many cyber-attacks, the weakest point is not the computer. It is the human being 
using the computer.
4.4 Password Attacks
Attackers may try to gain access by stealing, guessing or cracking passwords.
Example
Using a weak password such as:
Sbis1234
makes it easier for an attacker to guess compared with a strong and unique password.
4.5 Denial-of-Service (DoS) Attack
A Denial-of-Service attack attempts to make a system or website unavailable to legitimate 
users.
The attacker overwhelms the system with excessive requests or traffic.
Example
Imagine a website can normally handle 10,000 visitors.
An attacker sends millions of unnecessary requests. The server becomes overloaded, and 
genuine users cannot access the website.
This affects Availability.

slides.text:
SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
4.6 Insider Threat
An insider threat comes from someone inside an organization who has legitimate access to 
information or systems.
This may be:
● An employee
● A former employee
● A contractor
● Another authorized user
The threat may be intentional or accidental.
Example 1: Intentional
An employee deliberately copies customer data and sells it.
Example 2: Accidental
An employee accidentally sends confidential company information to the wrong person.
5. Cyber-Attacks
A cyber-attack is an intentional attempt to:
● Access a system without authorization
● Steal information
● Damage data
● Disrupt services
● Gain financial or other benefits
A simple attack process can be understood as:
Find a weakness → Exploit the weakness → Gain access → Perform harmful 
activity
Example

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
A company uses weak passwords.
An attacker discovers this weakness, gains access to an employee's account and then steals 
confidential customer information.
6. Security Controls
Security controls are measures used to prevent, detect or reduce security risks. 
They help organizations protect their:
● Data
● Computers
● Networks
● Applications
● Users
Security controls can be broadly understood as:
1. Preventive controls
2. Detective controls
3. Corrective controls
6.1 Preventive Controls
Preventive controls try to stop an attack before it happens.
Examples
● Strong passwords
● Firewalls
● Multi-Factor Authentication
● Access control
● Employee security training
● Encryption
Example
A website requires both:

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
● Password
● OTP on the user's phone
This makes unauthorized access more difficult. Therefore, Multi-Factor Authentication acts as a
preventive control.
6.2 Detective Controls
Detective controls help an organization identify that a security incident has happened or is 
happening.
Examples
● Security monitoring
● Intrusion detection systems
● Audit logs
● Suspicious login alerts
Example
Suppose you normally log into your account from India, but suddenly someone attempts to log 
in from another country.
The system sends you an alert.
This is a detective control because it detects suspicious activity.
6.3 Corrective Controls
Corrective controls help an organization recover after a security incident.
Examples
● Data backups
● Disaster recovery
● System restoration
● Incident response procedures
Example

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
A ransomware attack encrypts a company's files.
The company removes the malware and restores its files from a secure backup. 
This is a corrective control.
6.4 Security Controls at Different Levels
Security is not only about installing antivirus software. Organizations use different types of 
controls.
Technical Controls 
These use technology. 
Examples:
● Firewalls
● Encryption
● Antivirus software
● Multi-Factor Authentication
Administrative Controls
These involve rules, policies and procedures. 
Examples:
● Security policies
● Employee training
● Password policies
● Access management procedures
Physical Controls
These protect physical resources. 
Examples:
● Security guards
● CCTV cameras
● Locked server rooms
● Biometric access

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
7. Privacy in Information Systems
Privacy refers to an individual's right to control how their personal information is collected, used, 
stored and shared.
Personal information may include:
● Name
● Phone number
● Email address
● Location
● Financial information
● Browsing behaviour
Example
Suppose a mobile application collects a user's location even when location data is unnecessary 
for its service.
This can create a privacy concern.
8. Privacy Issues in Information Systems
Common privacy issues include:
● Collection of excessive personal data
● Data sharing without permission
● Unauthorized access to personal information
● Data breaches
● Excessive tracking of users
● Using personal data for purposes not clearly explained
Example
A shopping website collects your name and address to deliver a product. That may be 
necessary.

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
However, if the website secretly shares your information with many unrelated organizations, this 
creates a privacy issue.
9. Ethical Issues in Information Systems
Ethics refers to principles that help us decide what is right and wrong.
In Information Systems, an action may be technically possible but still be ethically wrong.
Example
A company may have the technical ability to track every website visited by its employees. 
But the question is:
Should the company track everything?
This is an ethical question.
Common Ethical Issues
1. Privacy
Is personal information being collected and used fairly?
2. Accuracy
Is the information correct?
3. Ownership
Who owns digital information?
4. Access
Who should be allowed to access information?

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
Example
Suppose a company collects customer data for delivering products.
Later, it decides to use that data for another completely unrelated purpose without informing 
customers.
Even if the company can technically do this, the action may raise serious ethical concerns.
10. Difference Between Privacy and 
Security
These two concepts are closely related but different.
Security
Security focuses on protecting information from unauthorized access, loss or damage.
Privacy
Privacy focuses on how personal information is collected, used and shared.
Example
A company may have very strong security, but still have poor privacy practices.
Suppose a company securely stores customer data but collects much more personal 
information than necessary.
● The security may be strong.
● The privacy practice may still be questionable.
3.2 AI Ethics and Responsible AI
11. Meaning of AI Ethics

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
AI Ethics refers to the principles and values that guide the responsible development and use of 
Artificial Intelligence.
AI systems can affect important decisions involving:
● Education
● Employment
● Banking
● Healthcare
● Business
● Government services
Therefore, AI systems should not simply be judged by the question:
"Does the AI work?"
We should also ask:
"Does the AI work fairly, safely and responsibly?"
12. Major AI Ethics Issues
12.1 Bias and Fairness
Bias occurs when an AI system produces unfair or systematically unequal outcomes.
AI systems learn from data. If the data contains unfair patterns, the AI may reproduce those 
patterns.
Example
Suppose an AI system is trained using historical hiring data that mostly contains successful 
candidates from one particular group.
The AI may learn patterns that unfairly disadvantage other qualified candidates. 
Therefore:
Unfair data can lead to unfair AI decisions.

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
12.2 Transparency
Transparency means that the functioning and decisions of an AI system should be 
understandable to an appropriate extent.
Example
Suppose a bank uses AI to reject a loan application. 
The applicant asks:
"Why was my loan rejected?"
If nobody can explain the decision, there is a lack of transparency.
12.3 Accountability
Accountability means that individuals or organizations should be responsible for the outcomes 
of AI systems.
Example
A company uses an AI system to make an incorrect decision that seriously harms a customer. 
The company should not simply say:
"The AI made the decision, so nobody is responsible."
Humans and organizations remain responsible for how AI systems are designed, deployed and 
monitored.
12.4 Privacy
AI systems may require large amounts of data. 
Organizations must carefully consider:
● What data is being collected?
● Why is it needed?
● Who can access it?

rects.text: The company should not simply say:

slides.text:
SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
● How long will it be stored?
● Is personal information properly protected?
12.5 Safety and Reliability
AI systems should work reliably and should be properly tested before being used for important 
decisions.
Example
If an AI system provides incorrect information in a casual entertainment application, the impact 
may be small.
However, if an AI system makes an incorrect decision in a high-impact environment, the 
consequences can be much more serious.
Therefore, the required level of testing and human oversight depends on how important the AI 
system's decisions are.
13. Responsible AI
Responsible AI means designing, developing and using AI in a manner that is:
● Fair
● Safe
● Transparent
● Accountable
● Privacy-conscious
● Reliable 
In simple words:
Responsible AI means using AI in a way that benefits people while reducing 
unfairness, harm and unnecessary risks.
14. Principles of Responsible AI

rects.text: consequences can be much more serious.

slides.text:
SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
1. Fairness
AI should avoid unjust discrimination.
2. Transparency
Important AI decisions should be understandable and appropriately explainable.
3. Accountability
Humans and organizations should remain responsible for AI systems.
4. Privacy
Personal data should be handled responsibly.
5. Safety
AI systems should be tested and monitored.
6. Human Oversight
Humans should remain involved where AI decisions have significant consequences.
15. Simple Example of Responsible AI
Suppose a company uses AI to screen job applications. 
A responsible approach would include:
1. Checking whether the training data contains unfair patterns.
2. Testing the system for biased outcomes.
3. Reviewing how the AI makes recommendations.

19. Digital Governance
Digital Governance refers to the policies, rules, responsibilities and processes used to manage 
digital technologies and information responsibly.
It helps organizations decide:
● Who is responsible for digital systems?
● How should data be managed?
● What security rules should be followed?
● How should privacy be protected?
● How should AI be used responsibly?
● What should happen when a cybersecurity incident occurs?
20. Importance of Digital Governance
Digital governance helps organizations:
● Protect information
● Define responsibilities
● Manage cybersecurity risks
● Protect privacy
● Ensure ethical technology use
● Respond effectively to incidents
● Build trust with users and customers

22. Important Differences
Information Security vs Cybersecurity
Information Security is the broader concept of protecting information in any form.
Cybersecurity mainly focuses on protecting digital systems, networks, devices and digital 
information from cyber threats.
Example
Protecting a physical confidential document in a locked cupboard is part of Information 
Security.
Protecting an online database from hackers is part of Cybersecurity.
Threat vs Attack
Threat: A potential danger.
Attack: An actual attempt to exploit a weakness.
Example
A known software vulnerability is a potential threat.
A hacker actually exploiting that vulnerability is an attack.

Fig: B2B - Business Selling to Business
Explanation:
A B2B transaction usually flows through procurement portals or B2B marketplaces: the
buying business places a purchase order, the supplying business ships the goods, and payment
is settled between the two companies, often with negotiated pricing and longer sales cycles
than a typical consumer purchase.
Advantages / Benefits:
• Large order values: Bulk transactions mean higher revenue per sale than typical
consumer orders.
• Recurring relationships: B2B buyers often become long-term, repeat customers.
• Streamlined procurement: Digital portals speed up ordering, invoicing, and
reordering.
Disadvantages / Limitations:
• Longer sales cycles: Negotiation and approval steps make B2B deals slower to close.
• Complex integration needs: Buyers often expect the portal to connect with their own
ERP or procurement systems.
• Smaller customer base: Fewer potential buyers exist compared with the mass market
in B2C.
Examples:
• Example 1: A car manufacturer ordering steel sheets in bulk from a supplier via a B2B
portal.
• Example 2: A wholesaler selling stock to multiple retailers through IndiaMART or
Alibaba B2B.

slides.text:
Content-based filtering matches items to a user's own past preferences, while collaborative
filtering matches users with similar behaviour to each other; most large platforms combine
both into a hybrid engine that ranks final suggestions.
Advantages / Benefits:
• Increased sales/engagement: Relevant suggestions drive additional purchases or
watch time.
• Better discovery: Surfaces niche items a user might otherwise never find.
• Automatic personalisation: Scales individually tailored suggestions to millions of
users.
Disadvantages / Limitations:
• Cold-start problem: Hard to recommend well for new users or new items with no
history.
• Filter bubble: Can over-narrow variety by repeating similar suggestions.
• Popularity bias: Tends to favour already-popular items over new ones.
Examples:
• Example 1: Amazon showing 'customers who bought this also bought' suggestions.
• Example 2: Netflix showing a personalised homepage that differs per subscriber.
Applications:
• E-commerce: Suggesting related or complementary products.
• Streaming: Personalising watch/listen recommendations.
• Advertising: Targeting ads based on predicted interest.

slides.text:
Page 1
B2B, B2C & C2C
Detailed Explanation, Examples, Applications & Differences
1. Introduction
B2B, B2C and C2C are common business and e-commerce models. They describe the relationship between
the seller and the buyer. B2B means Business-to-Business, B2C means Business-to-Consumer, and C2C
means Consumer-to-Consumer.
2. B2B – Business to Business
Meaning: B2B is a business model in which one business sells products or services to another business. The
buyer may be a company, manufacturer, retailer, institution or other organization.
Simple Example: Intel → Laptop Manufacturer → Customer
Applications:
• Wholesale: manufacturers sell products in bulk to wholesalers or retailers.
• Manufacturing: companies buy raw materials, components and machinery from suppliers.
• Software and SaaS: businesses purchase CRM, accounting, cybersecurity and productivity software.
• Cloud computing: organizations purchase computing, storage and infrastructure services.
• Banking and finance: banks provide corporate loans, payment processing and business accounts.
• Supply-chain management: businesses purchase inventory, logistics and procurement services.
Key Characteristics:
• Customers are businesses or organizations.
• Orders and transaction values are generally larger.
• Sales cycles are usually longer and may involve negotiation.
• Contracts, customized pricing and long-term relationships are common.
• Buying decisions focus strongly on cost, efficiency, ROI and business requirements.
3. B2C – Business to Consumer
Meaning: B2C is a business model in which a business sells products or services directly to individual
consumers for personal use. It is the model most commonly experienced in retail and online shopping.
Simple Example: Business → Consumer → Personal Use
Applications:
• Online shopping: consumers buy clothing, electronics, books, groceries and other products.
• Food delivery: restaurants and food platforms serve individual customers.
• Entertainment: consumers purchase streaming, music or gaming subscriptions.
• Travel and tourism: individuals book flights, hotels and holiday packages.
• Banking: banks provide savings accounts, credit cards and personal loans.

Page 2
• Education: online education companies sell courses directly to students.
Key Characteristics:
• Customers are individual consumers.
• Transactions are generally smaller than B2B transactions.
• Purchasing decisions can be influenced by price, convenience, brand and emotion.
• Sales cycles are usually short.
• Advertising, promotions, customer experience and after-sales service are important.
4. C2C – Consumer to Consumer
Meaning: C2C is a business model in which one individual consumer sells a product or service to another
individual consumer. An online marketplace or platform often connects the buyer and seller.
Simple Example: Consumer A → Online Marketplace → Consumer B
Applications:
• Second-hand products: used phones, laptops, furniture, bicycles and other goods.
• Online marketplaces: individuals list products for other individuals to purchase.
• Auction platforms: consumers can sell products through bidding or auctions.
• Classified advertisements: individuals advertise products or services for sale.
• Ticket reselling: consumers may transfer or resell eligible tickets where permitted.
• Rental platforms: individuals can offer assets or spaces to other individuals through a platform.
Key Characteristics:
• Both buyer and seller are consumers.
• Online marketplaces commonly provide the platform.
• Products may be new, used or second-hand depending on the marketplace.
• Trust, ratings, reviews and seller reputation are important.
• Price negotiation may be common.

• Online marketplaces commonly provide the platform.
• Products may be new, used or second-hand depending on the marketplace.
• Trust, ratings, reviews and seller reputation are important.

Page 3
5. Difference Between B2B, B2C and C2C
Feature B2B B2C C2C
Full Form Business to Business Business to Consumer Consumer to Consumer
Seller Business Business Individual consumer
Buyer Business Individual consumer Individual consumer
Typical Order Size Large Small/medium Small/medium
Transaction Value Generally high Generally lower Varies
Decision Basis ROI, efficiency, cost Price, convenience, experience Price, trust, condition
Sales Cycle Usually long Usually short Usually short
Negotiation Common Less common Common
Relationship Long-term Repeat or short-term Mostly transaction-based
Marketing Professional/business marketing Mass and digital marketing Marketplace/reputation-based
Example Supplier → Company Retailer → Customer Person → Person
6. Real-Life Comparison Using a Laptop
B2B: A company purchases 100 laptops for its employees.
Laptop Manufacturer → Company
B2C: An individual purchases one laptop for personal use.
Laptop Retailer → Customer
C2C: An individual sells a used laptop to another person through a marketplace.
Consumer A → Marketplace → Consumer B
7. Advantages
B2B:
• Large transaction values
• Long-term customers
• Repeat orders
• Stable business relationships
B2C:
• Large customer market
• Fast transactions
• Direct customer feedback
• Strong opportunities for digital marketing
C2C:
• Easy selling of unwanted products
• Lower prices for buyers
• Wide marketplace reach
